@@138037439 <h> A Critique of Tribal Exegesis : A Refutation of Alan Shlemon 's " Jihad and War in Islam and Christianity " <p> Alan Shlemon , in his essay " Jihad and War in Islam and Christianity , " constructs a binary essentialism that insulates Christian and Jewish scriptures from structural violence whilst anchoring Islamic texts to an alleged trans-historical framework of terror . This paper constitutes a refutation of that thesis . Drawing upon modern critical hermeneutics , post-colonial theology , progressive Christian and Jewish scholarship , and contemporary empirical data on political violence , this analysis demonstrates that the Bible has been , and continues to be , systematically misinterpreted to generate , legitimise , and prosecute state violence on an unprecedented global scale . The primary argument is that contemporary manifestations of tribal and racist biblical interpretation -- specifically Christian Zionism , right-wing Jewish Zionism , and Western Christian nationalism -- actively incite the war-mongering and militarism of the world 's most powerful state actors , most notably the United States and Israel . The authentic , pacifist , and humanistic core of both Christianity and Judaism @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ To mitigate ongoing systemic atrocities , these violent , state-sanctioned hermeneutical frameworks must be critically dismantled and re-anchored in Jesus 's radical message of universal love , restorative justice , and global reconciliation . <p> In his essay " Jihad and War in Islam and Christianity , " self-styled Christian apologist Alan Shlemon advances a deeply problematic and historically inaccurate claim : that while the Bible may be misinterpreted and misused , Islam and the Quran are inherently terroristic and intolerant , with jihad as a central , normative theology of war . This paper systematically refutes Shlemon 's distortion point by point , demonstrating that biblical misuse has historically produced far greater brutality than any alleged Islamic exceptionalism , and that contemporary American and Israeli war-making is precisely driven by tribal , racist interpretations of scripture -- Christian Zionism , Jewish Zionism , and Christian nationalism -- that continue to incite violence against Palestinian people and the global south . <p> The thesis of this paper is threefold . First , the misuse of the Bible has generated , and continues to generate , structural and physical violence on @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ actions of Muslim-majority states , which remain , in Shlemon 's own implicit admission , comparatively feeble . Second , the authentic messages of Jesus and the prophetic Jewish tradition are fundamentally pacifist , just , and reconciliatory ; these have been systematically suppressed by tribal , imperialist readings of scripture . Third , all tribal religious views -- whether Christian Zionist , Jewish Zionist , Islamic extremist , Hindu nationalist , or Buddhist nationalist -- must be transformed into pacifist , non-violent , just , and benevolent frameworks that authentically document historical and contemporary biblical misuse and restore the prophetic core of each tradition . <p> Shlemon 's methodology suffers from a foundational error common in literalist apologetics : textual essentialism . He assumes that a text possesses an intrinsic , stable meaning independent of the historical , socio-political , and cultural matrices of its readers . Yet , as contemporary hermeneutical theorists note , scriptures do not function in a vacuum . They operate within what Stanley Fish calls " interpretive communities " that actively construct meaning based on prevailing power dynamics ( Fish , p.14 ) . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ as divine sanction for colonial expropriation , a liberation theologian reads as a cautionary tale about the corruption of political power . <p> Shlemon 's insistence that Old Testament violence is purely " descriptive " -- a one-time historical record with no prescriptive force -- whilst treating Islamic jurisprudential discussions of jihad as permanently normative , represents precisely the orientalist double standard theorised by Edward Said . As Karen Armstrong argues in Fields of Blood , " every major religion has been used to justify violence " and every tradition has simultaneously produced profound voices for peace ; the decisive factor is never the text itself but the social and political context of its reception ( Armstrong , p.9 ) . <p> Progressive biblical scholar Marc Ellis argues that the history of scriptural reception is a history of political contestation . A fair analysis , as multiple scholars have insisted , must apply identical hermeneutical standards to all traditions . <p> Irish biblical theologian Michael Prior further demonstrated that the biblical narrative of the Exodus from Egypt and the Conquest of Canaan had been deployed to justify colonialism in Palestine , the Americas , and South Africa . The former corrupts every tradition it inhabits ; the latter is the common patrimony of all ( Buber , p.45 ) . <p> Jonathan Sacks , in his more universalist moments , noted that " when religion turns men into murderers , God weeps " ( Sacks , p.210 ) . This applies with absolute impartiality . The God who weeps over jihadist atrocities weeps equally over crusading massacres , colonial genocides , the bombing of civilian populations in Gaza , and the theological cover given to these @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ selectively invoke divine weeping only for the sins of one tradition is to transform mourning into propaganda . <p> Stultifying Tribal Religion <p> The thesis of this paper demands not merely critique but construction . It is insufficient to document the misuses of the Bible without also articulating the positive hermeneutical principles that must replace them . The following principles , drawn from the scholars engaged throughout this analysis , constitute the foundation of a responsible , humanistic reading of Abrahamic scripture . <p> The cross of Jesus , understood not as a sacrificial transaction but as the paradigmatic enactment of non-violent love in the face of imperial violence , must function as the interpretive lens through which the entire biblical narrative is read . This means reading the Old Testament 's conquest narratives not as divine mandates for contemporary violence but as cautionary tales about the corruption of political power , and reading the New Testament 's social ethic not as accommodation to empire but as radical challenge to it . Wink 's insight that Jesus embodied " a third way " beyond both violence and passive submission provides @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ collaboration equally unacceptable . <p> The Hebrew prophets -- Amos , Hosea , Isaiah , Jeremiah , Micah -- consistently subordinate ritual observance , ethnic identity , and territorial claim to the demands of justice , mercy , and protection of the vulnerable . Micah 's summary -- " to do justice , and to love kindness , and to walk humbly with your God " ( Micah 6:8 ) -- is not an optional supplement to the covenantal promise but its moral core . Any reading of scripture that produces injustice for the vulnerable , dispossession of the weak , or contempt for the stranger has , by this prophetic standard , misread the text -- regardless of what proof-texts it marshals in its support . <p> The imago Dei -- the affirmation that every human being bears the image of God ( Genesis 1:27 ) -- is not a tribal affirmation of the dignity of one ethnic group but an absolute , universal claim . Any theology that conditions full human dignity on ethnic identity , national citizenship , religious affiliation , or any other contingent category has @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ This principle , taken seriously , renders every form of tribal exclusivism -- Christian Zionist , Jewish Zionist , Islamic extremist , or any other -- a theological impossibility , a direct contradiction of the text it claims to interpret . <p> Diana Eck 's concept of active pluralism -- not merely tolerating difference but engaging with it as a resource for spiritual and ethical growth -- provides the civic and theological framework within which reformed religious communities can coexist without violence . Active pluralism does not require the abandonment of particular commitments ; it requires that those commitments be held in a way that recognises the equal dignity and integrity of those who hold different ones . Eck 's Pluralism Project at Harvard has documented both the extraordinary religious diversity of contemporary societies and the extraordinary capacity for violence when that diversity is not respected . The transformation of tribal religion into active pluralism is not a theological luxury ; it is a civilisational imperative . <p> The Real Jesus , the Real Prophets , and the Imperative of Transformation <p> Alan Shlemon 's binary -- Islamic terror versus @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is a dangerous one . It is dangerous not merely because it misrepresents the history of Christianity and Judaism , but because it provides ideological cover for ongoing atrocities by deflecting moral scrutiny away from the most powerful actors in the contemporary world and directing it exclusively towards the most fragile . A world in which the violence of nuclear-armed superpowers is theologically sanctioned whilst the reactive violence of the dispossessed is held up as evidence of an irredeemably violent religion is not a world moving towards peace ; it is a world in which the language of religion is used to entrench the dominance of the powerful . <p> The scholars whose voices have been amplified throughout this paper -- Brueggemann , Crossan , Yoder , Wink , Hauerwas , Armstrong , Cone , Ruether , Ateek , Ellis , Butler , Eck , Raheb , Prior , Burge , Cannon , Jenkins , Tutu , Heschel , Kwok , Said , and Asad -- have devoted their careers to the patient , rigorous work of distinguishing authentic faith from its tribal distortions . They speak not from a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ are capable , but from a position of intimate acquaintance with how religions can be and have been corrupted by the demands of power . Their unanimous testimony is that the misuse of the Bible has been at least as lethal , as systemic , and as enduring as the misuse of any other sacred text -- and that the corrective must come from within the traditions themselves , through a radical return to the prophetic and pacifist core . <p> The authentic message of the historical Jesus -- love of enemies , non-retaliation , care for the marginalised , welcome of the stranger , reconciliation with the adversary -- is not the mainstream of Western Christianity . It is the counter-cultural , prophetic voice that has been systematically suppressed by imperial Christianity since the conversion of Constantine . The authentic message of the Hebrew prophets -- justice for the widow and the orphan , protection for the stranger and foreigner , the priority of righteousness over ritual and ethnic identity -- is not the mainstream of contemporary Jewish Zionism . It is the marginalised voice of those who insist @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the covenant of justice with humanity . <p> To stop the cycle of biblically incited violence , this paper calls for five concrete commitments : <p> * Authentic documentation of the historical and contemporary misuse of the Bible , without apologetic minimisation , so that religious communities can engage honestly with their own traditions . <p> * Amplification of the voices of progressive , pacifist , and humanistic scholars within both Christianity and Judaism , who represent the deepest ethical wisdom of their traditions rather than their tribal distortions . <p> * Rejection of all tribal religious views -- Christian Zionist , Jewish Zionist , Christian nationalist , or any other -- that condition divine favour upon ethnic identity or national membership . <p> * Solidarity with the oppressed , including but not limited to the Palestinian people , as the concrete political expression of the prophetic demand for justice . <p> * The cultivation of active religious pluralism , rooted in the recognition of the equal dignity of every human being and the equal integrity of every genuine spiritual tradition . <p> Shlemon is correct that the real Jesus @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ reconciliation . Where his argument fails are in assuming that Christianity is uniquely defined by its highest ideals while Islam is uniquely defined by its worst abuses . History does not support this conclusion . The same principle of hermeneutical charity must be extended to all traditions -- or denied to all . The real struggle is not between Christianity and Islam . It is between tribalism and universalism , between domination and justice , between the faith that seeks power over others and the faith that seeks genuine relation with God and neighbour . The future of all religions , and possibly of human civilisation itself , depends on strengthening interpretations rooted in compassion , equality , reconciliation , and human dignity , whilst marginalising every theology that sanctifies hatred , supremacy , or violence . @@138068359 <h> The Iran War and the Global Costs of Unpredictable Power <p> The events surrounding the Iran war over the past week again draw our attention to the unpredictable nature of the contemporary international dispensation . Within the span of a few hours , we have witnessed a dramatic turn from threats of ' very hard ' strike to statements of discussion and ' final points ' for peace . President Donald Trump first warned of devastating strikes against Iran , threatened to take control of Kharg Island -- the strategic hub of Iran 's oil exports -- and even spoke about assuming control over parts of Iran 's energy infrastructure . Later the same day , Trump announced that planned military operations had been cancelled because an agreement with Tehran was apparently close at hand . But Iran immediately pushed back , insisting that negotiations were still incomplete and that no final agreement had been reached . <p> This unusual sequence of events is certainly a part of the long history of tensions between Washington and Tehran , revealing a more worrying reality -- the growing volatility in global @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ more dictated by unexpected policy shifts , personal calculations , social media diplomacy , and unilateral decisions taken by a handful of leaders . The consequences of such behaviour go quickly through energy markets , shipping routes , financial systems , labour migration networks , and food supply chains . Ultimately , they arrive at the doorsteps of ordinary families . The Iran war demonstrates , again and again , how the actions and statements of a single leader in the White House can influence the lives of people across continents . <p> The war itself has now crossed more than three months . In a highly interconnected and interdependent world , the impact of wars taking place on faraway battlefields spreads through economic and social networks . A missile launched in the Gulf can affect the price of cooking gas in Kerala . A disruption in the Strait of Hormuz can alter freight rates in Asia and Africa . A political threat issued in Washington can trigger speculation in commodity markets across the globe . The Iran war , therefore , has become an important lesson about the nature @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ military frontlines . <p> The institutions established after the Second World War were designed to prevent precisely this kind of escalation . International treaties , diplomatic mechanisms , multilateral negotiations , and the United Nations emerged from the recognition that global stability requires rules , predictability , and cooperation . But , over years , these institutions have steadily weakened . Major powers increasingly ignore international law when it becomes difficult and inconvenient . Agreements are abandoned , diplomatic norms are discarded , and military force is often presented as the first rather than the last option . <p> Within this history of decline of multilateralism , Donald Trump 's approach to foreign policy has played a significant role . One of the most consequential decisions of his first presidency was the unilateral withdrawal from the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action ( JCPOA ) , commonly known as the Iran nuclear agreement . The agreement had emerged from years of negotiations involving the United States , European powers , Russia , China , and Iran . International inspectors repeatedly confirmed that Iran was complying with its obligations . But the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ maximum pressure " based on sanctions , economic coercion , and diplomatic isolation . The consequences were predictable . Instead of reducing tensions , the policy intensified mistrust . Instead of strengthening regional security , it increased instability . Diplomatic channels narrowed while confrontation expanded . The collapse of the JCPOA removed one of the few effective mechanisms for managing the conflict . The present war is the outcome of years of accumulated distrust , failed diplomacy , and escalating hostility . <p> The recent sequence of threats and reversals follows this pattern . Markets , governments , businesses , and citizens are left uncertain about what comes next . One presidential statement warns imminent war , another indicates an approaching peace agreement . Such volatility itself becomes a source of instability . Markets fluctuate and investors hesitate . Governments prepare for worst-case scenarios . Commodity traders speculate on future shortages . Families with relatives in conflict zones live with constant anxiety . Uncertainty becomes a force capable of generating real economic and social consequences . <p> Perhaps nowhere is this evident than in the Strait of Hormuz . This @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ oil and gas supplies , besides other commodities such as fertilisers and chemicals . Any threat to its security immediately affects global energy markets . During the Iran conflict , concerns about maritime disruption pushed oil prices upward , increased shipping costs , and raised insurance premiums for vessels operating in the region . These developments tell the extraordinary vulnerability of the global economy to geopolitical shocks . <p> For India , the implications are far-reaching . As one of the world 's largest importers of crude oil , India is highly dependent on stable energy supplies from the Gulf region . Rising oil prices have already increased inflationary pressures , strain public finances , and complicate economic planning . @@138068378 <p> When the International Network on Explosive Weapons ( INEW ) released its 2025 global report in May 2026 , it delivered a message the world can no longer ignore : explosive weapons in populated areas are reshaping the nature of conflict worldwide . From Latin America to Eastern Europe , from the Sahel to South Asia , and across the Arab region , urban bombardment has become a defining feature of modern warfare , with consequences that extend far beyond national borders . <p> INEW recorded more than 22,600 civilians killed by explosive weapons in 2025 . Humanitarian operations were hit 2,541 times . Education facilities were damaged or destroyed in 1,416 incidents.Health services were struck 1,272 times . Civilian harm was documented in 65 countries and territories , a clear sign that this is not a regional crisis but a global emergency . <p> The devastation is not limited to immediate casualties . When explosive weapons destroy homes , water systems , power grids , and hospitals , the effects cascade across borders and generations . Public health collapses . Epidemics spread more easily . Food insecurity deepens @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Trauma becomes a shared inheritance . <p> These patterns are visible worldwide . In Ukraine , the destruction of energy and health infrastructure has created long-term public-health risks . In Myanmar , bombardment of villages has driven mass displacement into neighboring countries . In the Sahel , explosive violence has accelerated the collapse of already fragile health systems . And in the Arab region ; including Gaza , Lebanon , Yemen , Sudan , and Syria , the compounded effects of repeated bombardment have pushed entire populations to the brink of survival . <p> These are not isolated tragedies . They are part of a global pattern in which explosive weapons are systematically degrading the health , stability , and resilience of societies . <p> But the most enduring impact is not physical . It is psychological and political . Repeated bombardment produces grief , anger , resentment , and a profound sense of injustice . These emotions shape collective memory , influence political behavior , and determine whether communities will trust or reject future peace efforts . Civilian harm today becomes the architecture of tomorrow 's conflict . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ protection erodes in one region , it weakens norms everywhere . When one state uses explosive weapons indiscriminately , others take note . When accountability fails in one conflict , it becomes harder to enforce in the next . The world is witnessing a dangerous normalization of urban warfare , and with it , a weakening of the international system designed to prevent mass suffering . <p> Legitimacy is at the heart of this challenge . INEW 's data shows that state armed forces were responsible for 85 percent of all incidents affecting civilians in 2025 . This underscores the urgent need for stronger global accountability mechanisms and for armed actors to adopt robust civilian-protection policies . Those who minimize harm , conduct transparent investigations , and cooperate with humanitarian and civil society organizations preserve political capital for future negotiations . Those who disregard civilian suffering accumulate a moral and strategic deficit that may haunt them long after the fighting ends . <p> Civil society and campaigners are central to reversing this global trajectory . From Latin America 's human-rights networks to African peace coalitions , from European disarmament groups @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , advocating for policy reform , supporting survivors , and preserving the social fabric that conflict seeks to tear apart . Their work is not peripheral . It is essential to rebuilding trust , restoring dignity , and laying the groundwork for peace . <p> The 2022 Political Declaration on Strengthening the Protection of Civilians from the Humanitarian Consequences Arising from the Use of Explosive Weapons in Populated Areas -- now endorsed by more than ninety states -- offers a critical global framework . The INEW report highlights areas of progress , including new national policies on harm mitigation and improved data collection . But it also shows that implementation remains uneven and that global enforcement , transparent reporting , and stronger partnerships with civil society are urgently needed . <p> History repeatedly shows that peace agreements are easier to sign than to sustain . Lasting peace depends on whether societies emerge from war with enough trust , legitimacy , and social cohesion to prevent renewed cycles of violence . Protecting civilians is therefore not only a humanitarian obligation ; it is the foundation on which durable peace is built @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . It begins with the choices made today about whether civilians are protected or sacrificed . Every bomb that destroys a home also destroys a portion of the trust upon which tomorrow 's peace depends , whether in Gaza , Khartoum , Kyiv , Port-au-Prince , or beyond . <p> Every civilian spared from explosive violence becomes part of humanity 's living legacy -- proof that compassion can outlast conflict . Protecting life today is how societies write their moral history , ensuring that future generations inherit not ruins , but the memory of restraint and the possibility of peace . <p> Protecting civilians is not charity . Trump 's initiative monetises reconstruction through US$1-billion membership fees while operating outside UN frameworks , yet faces hurdles , including a critical cash crunch and Hamas 's refusal to disarm . @@138094614 <h> Soft Digital Repression : New Challenges and Strategies for Resistance <p> During the recent assault on Gaza , thousands of activists witnessed their posts deleted or their accounts restricted simply for documenting Israeli occupation crimes or expressing solidarity with the Palestinian people . This is far from an isolated phenomenon . In India , the government issued emergency orders to block dozens of accounts during the farmers ' protests , while human rights organizations documented the suspension of accounts belonging to large numbers of journalists and activists merely for criticizing government policies . Many felt helpless and furious , as their voices seemed to be deliberately pushed to the margins . These cases offer a clear illustration of what can today be called ' soft digital repression . ' <p> This form of repression does not always manifest as direct blocking or public arrest . It operates through invisible algorithms and digital systems , reshaping the digital space in ways that determine what reaches audiences and what gets marginalized . With the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence , these mechanisms have grown increasingly complex and far-reaching . This raises @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and how can it be confronted ? <p> Digital Control and Voluntary Self-Surveillance <p> Large digital corporations collect vast amounts of data systematically , using artificial intelligence to analyze it and classify users according to behavioral patterns , intellectual orientations , and political inclinations . Through carefully designed algorithms , left-wing , progressive , and human rights content can be restricted without any need for direct deletion . From the user 's perspective , low engagement appears to stem from audience indifference , when in reality it may be the result of algorithmic mechanisms controlling the level of reach and visibility . <p> Many have experienced this firsthand : a significant post is written and reaches only a limited number of followers . Numerous studies have examined the phenomenon of the filter bubble , whereby users are gradually isolated within information environments that reinforce their pre-existing views while limiting their exposure to critical or alternative content . The 2021 Facebook leaks revealed internal discussions concerning content management and the influence of algorithms on the public sphere . The Brookings Institution has documented how digital platforms contribute to deepening political polarization @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ users begin practicing what might be called ' voluntary self-surveillance , ' imposing restrictions on themselves out of fear of bans or declining reach . This fear reshapes the nature of public discourse and gradually transforms the digital space into a more controlled environment , one that serves the interests of the forces dominating the digital infrastructure . <p> Digital Frustration <p> Through the constant flow of content , algorithms contribute to generating a sense of helplessness and loss of hope in the possibility of change , by repeatedly emphasizing the failures of progressive experiments and presenting the existing capitalist order as the only viable option . At the same time , individualism and personal success solutions are promoted as the primary path for addressing social problems , while consumer culture and individual achievement are presented as the practical alternative to collective action and political organization . The result is the isolation of individuals , the weakening of collective bonds , and the transformation of shared social concerns into personal responsibilities . <p> Digital Arrest and Digital Assassination <p> When covert surveillance or frustration proves insufficient , the system reaches @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ suddenly find their accounts suspended or blocked without prior warning , with these measures justified by generic phrases such as ' violating community standards , ' even though the targeted content is in many cases documentation of human rights violations or war crimes . <p> In other cases , the situation reaches what can only be described as ' digital assassination ' : the complete erasure of the digital presence of individuals or entire institutions . The targeting of Palestinian content stands as one of the most contested examples , with human rights organizations and researchers having documented numerous instances of post deletions and account restrictions linked to coverage of violations , alongside a striking inconsistency in the application of content rules across different parties . <p> What Can Be Done ? Alternatives for Left-Wing and Progressive Forces <p> If soft digital repression seeks to limit the potential for resistance , organization , and free expression , then confronting it begins with reconsidering technology itself as an arena of social and political struggle . <p> This requires pushing for greater transparency and democratic oversight of large digital corporations , and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and mandates disclosure of algorithmic decision-making mechanisms . <p> The response can not be limited to legislation alone . There is also a need to build digital left-wing internationals and cross-border solidarity networks that expose digital violations and defend rights and freedoms in the online space . Users and civil society institutions can also exert pressure on companies involved in developing or selling surveillance technologies used against activists , journalists , and dissidents . <p> It is equally important to support free and open-source software , and to develop alternative platforms that are more transparent and subject to community oversight , so that technology is used to protect rights , expose violations , and strengthen democratic participation . <p> Left-wing and progressive organizations should also develop their own digital tools , ranging from encryption and privacy protection technologies to awareness campaigns that expose the inner workings of algorithms and their political and social impact . <p> Technology Between Domination and Liberation <p> If the recurring experiences of Palestinian content restrictions , alongside other cases that have targeted left-wing , progressive , and human rights voices across different parts of the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ they also confirm that alternatives are possible . <p> The internet is not merely a global marketplace for advertising and data . It is a social , political , and cultural space that can contribute to building new forms of collective action and struggle for social justice . <p> For this reason , the battle over technology remains part of the broader struggle against domination and exploitation , and for democracy , equality , freedom , and a socialist alternative . Returning the human being to the center of digital decision-making remains a fundamental condition for building a future in which technology serves society rather than the accumulation of capital . <h> Subscribe to Our Newsletter <p> Rezgar Akrawi is a leftist writer and researcher focused on technology , AI , the digital revolution , and the development of contemporary leftist thought and practice in response to these transformations . @@138118049 <h> The Age of Disposable Peoples : An Indictment Before the Tribunal of History -- With Iran as Exhibit <p> Far from the polished rooms where men in suits explain the suffering of others in a language designed not to tremble . <p> I was born in the Sahara . <p> In a land where memory walks slowly , but never dies . <p> There , people learn early what empires spend centuries trying to hide : <p> When powerful men lie , ordinary people bury the dead . <p> This article is not written against a nation . <p> Not against a religion . <p> Not against a people . <p> It is written against an idea . <p> The most dangerous political idea of our century : <p> That some peoples are disposable . <p> Not officially . <p> No empire says this plainly . <p> No president signs a decree saying some children matter less . <p> No minister stands before cameras and declares that some nations have only conditional humanity . <p> Yet the world is governed , bombed , sanctioned and deceived as if this @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ humanity under rubble . <p> Lebanese civilians are asked to understand why their villages must become messages . <p> Iranians are discussed as a regime before they are remembered as a people . <p> Cubans are punished across generations for the crime of refusing obedience . <p> And always , the same mechanism returns . <p> First , a people becomes a problem . <p> Then the problem becomes a threat . <p> Then the threat becomes an exception . <p> Then the exception becomes policy . <p> Then policy becomes death . <p> Language performs the first act of violence long before the missile arrives . <p> The bomb merely completes what vocabulary has already begun . <p> In 1953 , Mohammad Mossadegh committed what empires have often considered the unforgivable crime : he believed Iranian oil belonged to Iranians . Operation Ajax followed . An elected prime minister was overthrown through a covert operation organized by the CIA and MI6 . Decades later , official documents confirmed what Iranians had never forgotten . <p> The lesson was simple . <p> Sovereignty was tolerated only when it remained harmless @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ninety miles from the most powerful country on earth . More than six decades of embargo followed . Presidents changed . Speeches changed . The Cold War ended . The Soviet Union disappeared . The punishment remained . <p> Generations were born under sanctions , grew old under sanctions , and died under sanctions . <p> The policy lasted longer than many of the people it claimed to influence . <p> Then came Iraq . <p> The world was told that weapons of mass destruction existed . <p> They did not . <p> The invasion happened anyway . <p> The dead did not return when the lie collapsed . <p> That is the privilege of imperial falsehood : it can be corrected after the cemetery is full . <p> Then came the JCPOA . <p> Iran negotiated . Inspectors inspected . Commitments were verified . Diplomacy , for once , appeared to have built a narrow bridge over a dangerous abyss . <p> Then the United States walked away . <p> Not because the bridge had collapsed . <p> But because power changed hands . <p> For millions across the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ may be signed , honored and verified -- and still be destroyed by the next ruler of the empire . <p> What , then , is diplomacy worth when the powerful reserve the right to betray yesterday 's signature ? <p> Gaza may become the defining moral trial of the twenty-first century . <p> Not because history lacks other tragedies . <p> But because never before has so much suffering been visible in real time . <p> A sovereign country repeatedly treated as a battlefield by powers larger than itself . <p> Its villages become warnings . <p> Its skies become corridors . <p> Its civilians become pressure points . <p> Its sovereignty becomes negotiable whenever force requires a map . <p> And then came Iran again . <p> The war of 2026 revealed something more frightening than military violence . <p> It revealed war as performance . <p> One day , unconditional surrender . <p> The next day , imminent peace . <p> One day , victory . <p> The next day , escalation . <p> One day , a deal . <p> The next day , fire . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ He stripped it of ceremony . <p> Older empires wrapped domination in doctrine . <p> Trump wrapped it in impulse . <p> He did not merely lie . <p> He made contradiction a method of government . <p> Of all the chapters in this indictment , this one is not yet closed . It is being written now , in real time , and it deserves more than a paragraph -- because for once , the method is not buried in archives or redacted cables . It is on the record , in his own words , this year . What follows is that record , read into evidence . <p> EXHIBIT ONE : THE CALENDAR OF CONTRADICTION <p> Look at four days in March , and the method stands naked . <p> On March 6 , he decreed there would be no deal " except for UNCONDITIONAL SURRENDER " -- and attached to the ultimatum an advertising slogan : Make Iran Great Again . On March 7 , he announced to the world that Iran had apologized and surrendered . The war , it seemed , was over . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , and Fury , " a response " twenty times " more violent . On March 10 , he demanded the " immediate " removal of mines from the Strait of Hormuz -- while admitting , in the same breath , that he had " no report " establishing they were ever there . <p> Surrender obtained . Then war reignited . Then apocalypse promised . Then an ultimatum built on a fact its own author admits does not exist . When a reporter asked , simply , to whom Iran was supposed to surrender -- no American soldier stood on Iranian soil -- the White House spokesperson gave away the whole architecture : the president alone would decide , whenever he wished , that Iran had " surrendered . " Surrender is no longer a fact . It is a mood . Reality has been dismissed . Only the decree remains . <p> But the dead do not get to be reissued . They stay dead under whichever version of the story is currently being told . <p> EXHIBIT TWO : THE GRAMMAR OF EMPIRE <p> Behind the clown @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ merely erratic -- it hardens into a doctrine of who is permitted to be sovereign , and who is not . <p> Trump did not only demand Iran 's surrender . He demanded a say in choosing Iran 's next Supreme Leader , calling for the " selection of a GREAT and ACCEPTABLE leader . " Acceptable to whom ? To him . A foreign president appointing himself arbiter over the spiritual leadership of a nation of ninety million people -- this is the unbroken grammar of colonialism , in which the native is never quite mature enough to govern himself . <p> Then he turned to the Kurds . Asked how the regime might fall without American boots on the ground , he called a Kurdish offensive into Iran " wonderful " : " I 'd be all for it . " He reportedly promised Kurdish leaders " extensive air cover " for an uprising . This is empire 's oldest maneuver : arm a minority against the state you wish to break , then abandon it once its use is exhausted -- as Washington has done to the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ since the 1970s . One does not treat peoples this way . One treats pawns this way . <p> And then , almost as an aside , he said the part usually left unsaid . Discussing the men his strikes had killed , he told reporters that most of the intended targets were already dead , and that soon , " we 're not going to know anybody . " The casualness is the racism . When the deaths of the Other stop being a tragedy and become a passing joke , the Other has already stopped being counted as human . This is what Malek Bennabi pointed toward with his idea of colonisabilit ? -- not the colonized 's real inferiority , but the colonizer 's settled conviction that he is dealing with matter , not with a people . <p> And this is where the miscalculation lives . Trump believed that killing Khamenei would collapse the regime , that the war would be folded in " four to five weeks . " He mistook a state for a man . You can not decapitate a nation the way @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ not dissolve a body woven from a historical solidarity no missile can reach . Iran did not plead . It closed the Strait . <p> EXHIBIT THREE : ONE MAN , ONE AIRPORT <p> One man . One airport . One administrative decision . Yet symbols matter -- and this time , the symbol was watched not by armies , but by billions . <p> Omar Abdulkadir Artan , a Somali referee named the Confederation of African Football 's referee of the year for 2025 , was to become the first Somali ever to officiate at a World Cup . He arrived in Miami from Istanbul carrying a valid U.S. visa , issued the week before . A former Somali diplomat noted that Artan had no criminal record and posed no threat @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a hero 's welcome -- wrapped in his country 's flag , carried by a crowd that , having no team to celebrate , celebrated one of its own . <p> Should this surprise anyone ? A sitting member of Congress , born in Somalia , was handed the same word . This was not the overreach of one zealous officer at a desk . It was presidential doctrine , spoken at the summit of the state , arriving -- mechanically , predictably -- at a checkpoint in Miami . <p> And the thread runs back to Iran , as everything in this story does . Trump had first threatened to bar Iran 's team from the tournament outright , until FIFA objected . It is propaganda with better manners . <p> Tehran 's government is no immaculate victim . One condemns it to choose between two jailers . <p> EXHIBIT SIX : THE SEA THAT DOES NOT OBEY <p> The Strait of Hormuz exposed the fraud . <p> A president can announce control . @@138134500 <p> A month ago , the Chief Justice of India remarked , in passing , that jobless young Indians who turn to activism behave like cockroaches . He clarified soon enough that he had meant only those who enter professions on fake degrees . But the word had already skittered out of reach . Frustrated young Indians picked it up , wore it , and turned the insult into a banner . On the evening of 6 June , hundreds swarmed New Delhi 's Jantar Mantar with national flags for the first rally of the new Cockroach Janta Party . The protests have since reached Maharashtra . <p> That a protest of this scale was permitted at all is reassuring . Though a democracy permitting its citizens ' dissent is fulfilling a duty , not doing them a favour . When the State forgets that duty , the citizen 's recourse is a court of law . Now , the Cockroach Janta Party got its permission . Many protesters never do , and many more are dragged into court by someone bent on shutting them down . That leaves a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ more durable one : when a protest matter reaches a High Court , how does the Indianjudicial system actually treat it ? <p> From TheProfesseer 's dataset , we sampled 136 matters before the Bombay and Delhi High Courts between 2021 and 2026 , in which the court ruled on a protest : its permission , its policing , its removal , or its punishment . <h> Who are India 's cockroaches ? <p> Mostly , India 's protesters are singular individuals who file their own cases . Across jurisdictions , they move the court in 76 per cent of the matters . They mostly ask for a venue , for protection , or for an FIR to be quashed . <p> While this is unsurprising , who makes up the rest usually goes unnoticed . In Delhi , more than a third of protest cases are filed not by a protester but by someone determined to shut one down : a resident 's association , a school , liquor stores ensconced in glass , and occasionally , a political outfit disguised in NGO clothing asking the court to clear @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ clash of citizens than a trade remedy ; average Kumars trying to get to work . <p> Graphic : Jeyasri AT , ThePrint <h> What cockroaches want <p> Our protesters , in court at least , are not as ambitious as one would imagine . Their aims are not the caricature painted of them -- some overzealous pursuit to topple a regime or to sweep an election at home . Their requests are smaller , nationally-rooted , and far more , if you will , human . <p> In Delhi , the case-titles read like a roll-call of the decade 's causes : Himalayan statehood , a farmers ' revolt over crop prices and poor water supply , bonded labour , and soldiers seeking their pension . <p> In Bombay High Court , Shiv Sena ( UBT ) had to sue the city to hold its Dussehra rally at Shivaji Park , and the court found the municipality had " misused its powers " . Months later , when the CPI(M) asked to march against the war in Gaza , the same court first told it to " be patriots @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ granted permission anyway . On aggregate , these fights are outliers . Two-thirds of Mumbai 's protest cases deal with property , largely from an anti-encroachment drive in Pimpri-Chinchwad 's Kudalwadi , where owners of unauthorised scrap godowns blockaded bulldozers and went to court to stop the demolition . <p> Graphic : Jeyasri AT , ThePrint <p> Also read : <h> What awaits the cockroaches in courts ? <p> In most of these cases , by the time a matter approaches the court as dispute , either a protest has elapsed and someone has had a grievance about the way it was conducted , or , alternatively , a protest was denied permission by the police and the rejection is contended . We only ever meet the cockroaches caught in the light . The ones that scurried off unbothered never trouble a cause-list . Therefore , the inherent selection of cases that reach courts that makes it a poor proxy for the general protest-friendliness of the Indian state . <p> Furthermore , to side with a protester , a court must also take an affirmative stance for the demonstration -- @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ yet , it often does , especially if the protester is the first mover . Challenge a wrongful FIR , an externment , or a refused permission , and the protester wins about seven times in 10 . At the same time , should a third party or the State bring a matter against an ongoing protest -- claiming that it is irregular or unlawful , the petitioners win 19 out of 20 times . In other words , the judicial prior tilts in favour of the first mover within our sample . This reveals less about judicial trends and owes more to the invisible factors at play . Who ends up becoming the first mover of a court is multicausal and impossible to triangulate with just court orders . <p> However , at their best , Indian courts encourage legitimate protests with enviable conviction . In a suo motu matter before the Nagpur bench of the Bombay High Court , the judges held with no ambiguity that peaceful protests are a crucial component of fundamental rights under Article 19 and directed the State to arrange shelter and welfare for @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ spirit , in Sharad Ramdas Mali v. State of Maharashtra , the Aurangabad bench quashed an FIR registered against a protester simply for taking part in an agitation . Better still , in Vijayabai Vyankat Suryawanshi v. State of Maharashtra , the court directed an FIR against the police officers alleged to be responsible for the custodial death of a peaceful protester -- the petitioner 's son . The Bombay High Court does not shy from admonishing the civic authorities when they overstep either . In Shiv Sena v. Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai , it found the Corporation had misused its powers in refusing permission for a rally . It has shown no hesitation , at times , in striking down police notices that deny permission to demonstrate outright , as it did across a string of matters from Parbhani ( Sawrate v. the District Magistrate ) . <p> But for every such defence of the right to protest , there are several instances the other way . In the Kudalwadi encroachment cases -- where traders , mostly migrant and Muslim , had worked for decades and received no @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Court refused the protesters ' pleadings in a breath . Illegal construction , it held , can not be protected by gathering a crowd . In East Delhi Municipal Corporation v. Commissioner of Police , the Delhi High Court described striking sanitation workers as " mischievous and unruly persons who take the law into their hands " and who " do not deserve leniency " . The court may well have had reason , given that the workers had reportedly strewn garbage in public spaces and stopped their non-striking colleagues from working . However , harsh language that extends to the description of safai karamcharis as " unruly persons " is concerning . <p> That our window of study opens only in 2021 implies that it necessarily misses the protests that still haunt this decade 's courtrooms . Prosecutions initiated at the sit-in at Shaheen Bagh , the accused of Bhima Koregaon , and several other matters that grind on as undertrials long after the placards came down , lie outside the scope of our examination . At least one side of the Indian public does believe that the courts @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ protesters than for the protests themselves . <p> Whatever one makes of the politics , one may still ask whether the full might of the State needed to fall on an octogenarian priest who died awaiting bail , or on a pregnant woman held under an anti-terror law . For all the nuclear fallouts that they are famed to survive , cockroaches are not immune to the State 's indiscriminate extermination . The court 's liberalism and generosity are the only hope for well-meaning civilians to prevail . As testament to their resilience , right across the street in Nepal , we see stifled youth movements erupting doubly strong , replacing the very powers that once swept them under the carpet . As ancient wisdom goes , a republic that treats its peaceful , lawful protest as integral rather than incidental , belittles none and hears all ; and a judiciary willing to say as much , out loud , keeps its arthropods happy . <p> Srikanth Rajkumar is a Developer and Data Scientist at TheProfesseer . @@138145264 <h> The Conversation No One Was Meant to Hear <h> Mearsheimer , Karaganov , and the Return of the Unthinkable Nuclear Option in the European Strategic Theatre <p> Some interviews illuminate a single event . Others illuminate an entire era . The conversation between Glenn Diesen , John Mearsheimer , and Sergey Karaganov 13 belongs to the rarer category : the kind of historical document that lets us hear , almost unfiltered , what official doctrines normally conceal beneath the cold language of strategy . <p> For nearly two hours , two of the most prominent figures in contemporary geopolitical thought discussed something that , only a few years ago , would have been unspeakable : the possibility of a limited nuclear strike against the European security architecture as a means of restoring deterrence . <p> What is most disturbing is not only what was said . What is most disturbing is that it can now be said publicly . Because when an idea enters the strategic mainstream , it is often because it has already been circulating for some time within the corridors of power . <p> A Fear @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ premise : the world has entered the most dangerous period of its modern history . Not because the weapons are new , but because the old fear has disappeared . <p> For decades , he argues , relative peace was not secured by human wisdom , nor by international morality , nor by multilateral institutions . It was secured by the fear of nuclear hell -- the fear of annihilation , of cities vanishing , of the irreversible . <p> That fear , in his view , has weakened in the West . NATO , he suggests , has progressively tested Russian thresholds : tanks , heavy artillery , HIMARS , F-16s , long-range missiles , satellite intelligence , deep strikes inside Russian territory , attacks on strategic infrastructure . At every stage , the Western assumption appeared to be the same -- Moscow would protest , but would never actually cross its own red lines . <p> Karaganov argues that this assumption has become lethal . If an adversary no longer believes in your capacity for destruction , deterrence ceases to exist . Fear , in his logic , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ reasoning becomes chilling . After a sequence of conventional escalation steps , he raises the idea of a limited nuclear strike on the European theatre -- not to conquer , not to occupy , but to psychologically force the West to back down . <p> It bears emphasizing that this idea is morally monstrous , and Karaganov himself acknowledges that it would open a Pandora 's box . But its real significance lies elsewhere : it signals that a segment of Russian strategic thought now treats nuclear weapons not merely as instruments of non-use , but as potential tools of coercion . <p> It is also worth situating Karaganov 's role more precisely . He is not an isolated commentator improvising on camera . For several years he has openly advocated , in published essays , for so-called " sobering " or " educational " strikes against Western targets -- arguments that predate this interview by some time 10 . In that sense , his rhetoric functions less as speculative theorizing than as a deliberate probing of Western tolerance thresholds : say the unsayable , observe the reaction , and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ exchange of views misses that function entirely . <p> Mearsheimer and the Forgotten Lessons of the Cold War <p> John Mearsheimer does not endorse the notion of nuclear " victory . " He restates a truth that current generations seem to have forgotten : a full-scale nuclear war has no winner . Everyone ends up vaporized . <p> But he agrees with Karaganov on one essential point -- the West has lost the culture of prudence that defined the Cold War era . <p> During that period , Washington and Moscow understood where the red lines were . The crises over Berlin , Cuba , Hungary , and Czechoslovakia were dangerous , but leaders on both sides knew there existed a threshold beyond which politics ended and annihilation began . <p> Today , Mearsheimer says he is stunned by the West 's strategic carelessness . He points specifically to the Ukrainian incursion into Russia 's Kursk region , as well as strikes targeting elements connected to Russia 's nuclear triad . During the Cold War , he suggests , no one in Washington would have played with that kind of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ cornering a nuclear power is extremely dangerous . A great power holding thousands of warheads can not be treated as an ordinary state . One can not attempt -- without risking systemic consequences -- to expel Russia from the rank of great powers , dismantle its economy , encircle it militarily , and strike its strategic territory . <p> The problem , then , is not purely military . It is cognitive . The West appears to have forgotten that Russia can lose a great deal -- but can not accept what it perceives as an existential defeat . <p> The European Theatre as a Theoretical Firing Range <p> The most unsettling part of the conversation concerns the European strategic theatre itself . <p> Karaganov starts from a blunt premise : the United States would likely not sacrifice New York for Warsaw , Chicago for Berlin , or Washington for Vilnius . In other words , the American nuclear guarantee would remain credible only up to the point where honoring it meant accepting the destruction of American territory . <p> This is not a new hypothesis -- it has haunted @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the context of the war in Ukraine gives this old question a chilling new urgency . <p> Mearsheimer understands the logic but underscores its consequences . If the United States failed to respond to a limited Russian strike on Europe , then Germany , Poland , or other European states might conclude that they need their own independent nuclear arsenals . <p> This is the point at which the conversation pivots toward the old " German question . " <p> Since 1945 , the European order has rested on an unwritten formula : contain Russia , restrain Germany , and keep the United States anchored at the center . The American military presence in Europe was never only about protecting Europe from Moscow -- it was also about managing German power itself . <p> That framework is now eroding . The United States is pivoting toward Asia to confront China . The European security architecture is being pushed to rearm at a historic pace . Since the 2022 " Zeitenwende " announcement and its 2025 acceleration , Germany has created special defense funds and announced one of the largest military @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ over a European nuclear umbrella -- partly anchored in French deterrence -- has gained momentum . Russia , whose strategic memory still carries the trauma of the Nazi invasion , watches this trajectory with something approaching existential unease . In the Russian strategic imagination , a rearming Germany is never simply " another European country " ; it is the reopening of a historical wound that 1945 was supposed to have permanently closed . <p> The Real Nuclear Landscape <p> To grasp the gravity of this conversation , one has to step outside the Ukrainian theater and look at the global nuclear landscape as a whole -- not as an inventory of arsenals , but as a map of how each power is responding to the same underlying problem that Karaganov diagnoses : the erosion of fear . <p> Call it the half-life of nuclear fear . Like a radioactive isotope , the lived memory of nuclear catastrophe decays over time , generation by generation , unless it is periodically renewed by crisis . What the conversation between Mearsheimer and Karaganov illustrates is not a sudden Russian aberration , but @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ every nuclear power : as the experiential memory of Hiroshima and the Cuban Missile Crisis fades , states increasingly compensate through doctrine rather than through restraint . Call this doctrinal overcompensation -- the tendency of declaratory policy to harden precisely as experiential deterrence weakens . The survey that follows can be read through this single lens : each country 's posture reveals where it sits on this curve , and how it is trying to slow its own decay . <p> The world is not simply returning to the Cold War . It is entering a far more unstable configuration -- more actors , more doctrines , more ambiguity , more shifting thresholds -- precisely because more states are independently attempting the same compensatory maneuver , each convinced that its own doctrine alone can hold back the fading of fear . <p> Russia revised its nuclear doctrine in November 2024 2 . It now states that nuclear use could be considered not only in response to a nuclear attack , but also in response to a conventional attack that threatens the existence of the state -- including cases where a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . The message to NATO is unambiguous : Ukraine ceases to be " just Ukraine " the moment it strikes using Western-supplied architecture . Russia 's 2024 revision is the clearest case of doctrinal overcompensation in action : unable to rely on the West 's intuitive fear of escalation , Moscow chose to write that fear into law . <p> The United States , for its part , continues to reject a " no first use " pledge . Its 2022 doctrine states that nuclear weapons would be considered only in " extreme circumstances " to defend the vital interests of the United States , its allies , and its partners 3 . This ambiguity is deliberate -- it reassures allies while leaving a zone of strategic uncertainty intact . Washington 's enduring vagueness is the inverse strategy to Moscow 's : rather than spelling out new thresholds , the United States treats uncertainty itself as the renewable resource of fear . <p> France maintains a doctrine of strict sufficiency , with the decision resting solely with the President of the Republic . Yet in March 2026 , Paris explicitly @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that France 's vital interests " have a European dimension " 4 . This does not mean sharing the nuclear button -- it means France is politically formalizing the idea that its vital interests carry a continental dimension . Paris 's move is best read as anticipatory : rather than wait for the American guarantee 's credibility to decay further , France is positioning its own deterrent to fill the coming gap . <p> The United Kingdom retains a minimal , credible , and independent deterrent based on its Trident submarines , while assigning it to NATO 's defense 5 . London deliberately maintains ambiguity about the precise circumstances of use -- denying any adversary the ability to calculate the British threshold with confidence . <p> Israel remains the most opaque case of all . Its official doctrine is silence : neither confirmation nor denial . Open-source estimates place its arsenal at approximately 90 warheads 6 . Its nuclear ambiguity is itself a doctrine , resting on the premise that an adversary should never know precisely where the threshold of the irreversible lies . <p> Ukraine , by contrast , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ inherited from the USSR under the 1994 Budapest Memorandum , in exchange for security assurances 7 . And yet the world is once again speaking about nuclear weapons with a growing -- and troubling -- doctrinal casualness . <p> Arsenals are being modernized . Budgets are rising . Arms control treaties are unraveling . Communication channels between major powers are narrowing . Doctrines are hardening .
