It is another fortress model Iran must have examined with all diligence due . <h> The Impending Montreux of the Gulf <p> The proliferation of cheap , highly advanced asymmetric warfare capabilities -- anti-ship ballistic missiles ( ASBMs ) , explosive loitering munitions , and unmanned underwater vehicles ( UUVs ) -- has fundamentally disrupted traditional blue-water naval power projection . For the United States , which had built its global military strategy around massive , capital-intensive carrier strike groups , this shift has already created severe operational vulnerabilities , particularly in narrow maritime chokepoints such as Bab-el-Mandab and Hormuz . <p> As became obvious with every passing week since 28 February , Iran 's ' Hormuz gambit ' could no longer be resolved by the American Fifth Fleet attempting to enforce freedom of navigation mandates that were sounding anachronistic in the Fortress World @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ground -- two legal systems in permanent collision , a global energy system that could not function without the strait , and a middle-power coalition increasingly unwilling to absorb the costs of American maritime hegemony -- all pointed in the same direction . The Strait of Hormuz will not return to the post-1945 illusion of a demilitarised , frictionless multilateral commons . Geopolitical physics dictates a more realist resolution . <p> Iran 's play is , in its essential architecture , a ' Montreux-isation ' of Hormuz . It has proceeded in three phases . The first was the creation of a prohibitively ' uninsurable ' environment : by maintaining sufficient threat through drone swarms , naval harassment , and the selective seizure of tankers , Iran made ' free passage ' economically fictional . The Lloyd 's of London 's Joint War Committee 's war-risk designations , not Iranian naval orders , then performed the work of a blockade far more effective than the US tried to counter using its fleet. 32 Iran now does not need to even fire a single shot to achieve the de-facto exclusion it @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ let the insurance markets do the rest . <p> The second phase could now be the construction of a Permitted List : bilateral arrangements with sympathetic nations that guarantee safety of passage in exchange for quiet acknowledgment of Iranian regulatory authority . China has vetoed UN Security Council resolutions condemning Iranian maritime actions , and even when it abstained it argued that the proposed resolutions were unbalanced and failed to address the root causes of the conflict. 33 India , for its part , has deployed destroyers to escort its own vessels while declining to join any US-led coalition , tacitly accepting the partition of maritime governance . Saudi Arabia , meanwhile , has signed a US$7-billion currency swap with China , 34 quietly loosening the petrodollar tie that once made American protection seem worth its price . <p> It is difficult to predict when , but the third phase seems to be inching towards exhaustion and capitulation as a ceasefire that was no ceasefire , yet kept getting a new lease , finally concluded in a much hyped " deal " that in effect was little more than a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ conflict are expected to continue testing each other 's resolve indefinitely during this process . Eventually , just as Europe yielded to Ankara in 1936 not from legal conviction but from the sheer unsustainability of managing a security crisis without Turkish cooperation , the global order could find itself unable to sustain the economic cost of an unmanaged , unpredictable siege in Hormuz . <p> What could be a proposed framework for such a Hormuz Convention ? For Iran it would mirror its HOPE initiative , pushed considerably further. 35 Grant Iran and Oman , and maybe other regional powers too , should they agree to a security architecture independent of the United States , joint regulatory authority through a ' Hormuz Maritime Authority ' . Replace UNCLOS transit passage with the 1958 innocent passage framework , requiring advance notification for warship transit , and effectively ban the nuclear-powered ships that constitute the backbone of the US Fifth Fleet . Any ' Hormuz Lake ' strategy that lacks Omani participation will be legally incomplete . Oman has historically maintained a studied independence from Tehran 's embrace , underwritten by British and American security guarantees . Yet to treat this posture as permanent may be to misread the lessons Muscat and other regional actors have drawn from a decade of escalating regional crises in which they have often been cast as hapless negotiators between parties who can only talk at ( never to ) each other . They need third parties . <p> The mechanism of Oman 's and the region 's recalibration may be neither sudden nor ideological , but the cumulative mathematics of disillusionment . Muscat must have watched the US-Israel combine launch wars across the region -- wars whose costs fell entirely on @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Omani loyalty absorbed none of the consequences . The back-channel negotiations Oman hosted between Washington and Tehran -- services Muscat provided precisely because of its studied neutrality -- produced no durable settlement ; the Americans walked away , sanctions were tightened , and the missiles multiplied . <p> For many a small state positioned astride the world 's most contested waterway , the calculus may have shifted decisively : Western security architecture delivered diminishing returns while their entanglements multiplied . Oman 's and Qatar 's historical tradition of pragmatic neutrality may , paradoxically , be the quality that makes them most susceptible to Iran 's arguments for a new regional security architecture . A posture of cooperative strait management , shared with the other littoral state and insulated from great-power rivalry , could be a natural extension . <p> The broader reaction of the ' middle powers ' is , in geopolitical terms , the most consequential development of all . T ? rkiye , Indonesia , India , Saudi Arabia , and South Africa are not unified by ideology ; they are unified by a single strategic calculation : @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ security subscription while absorbing the consequences of American geopolitical choices become economically and politically untenable ? 37 Saudi Arabia 's currency hedging , Indonesia 's refusal to lift nickel export bans despite US pressure , India 's deployment of naval escorts for its own vessels , T ? rkiye 's gas brokerage operations -- these are not random acts of defiance . They are the tacit expressions of an emergent ' cartel of the non-aligned ' whose winning condition is a world where they can trade with China , buy weapons from Russia , and sell to the United States without asking permission from any of them . <p> The ' Donroe Doctrine ' -- the fusion of the Monroe Doctrine'sc sphere-of-influence logic with contemporary American transactionalism -- simultaneously hands Iran its most powerful legal argument and resolves a glaring internal contradiction : if Washington has retreated to ' Fortress America , ' treating the Eastern Hemisphere as a marketplace rather than a protectorate , why would it put ships at risk to enforce a freedom of navigation mandate that benefits Asian energy consumers rather than American ones ? The @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , as already stated far too often by America now , eventually , it will not . A transactional America should have no rational incentive to maintain the Fifth Fleet as a perpetual public good for Taiwan , India , Japan , China , and South Korea . The logical conclusion of the Donroe Doctrine is not hostility towards a Hormuz regulatory authority ; it is quiet acquiescence in one that compels import-dependent Asian nations to negotiate their own transit arrangements and bear their own security costs . Iran 's response -- If you do n't want China in the Caribbean , why should we want the US in the Persian Gulf ? -- has a structural coherence the architects of the original Monroe Doctrine would recognise ; and its transactional successor would add : If Asian nations want their molecules , let them pay for the passage . The consequence could be the emergence of an Indo-Pacific arc of dependence , a coalition of Hormuz-reliant import economies whose shared vulnerability compels a new regional energy security architecture. d <p> While a formal diplomatic convention may not be agreed to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the " Deal " to negotiate , signed between the presidents of Iran and the United States -- the power shift instigated by Iran 's defiance may well pass into de-facto practice well before it crystallises into de-jure convention . Energy-dependent nations will accept almost any terms of passage -- including Iran 's right to regulate and tax transits -- as long as those terms guarantee access to the oil and gas molecules their economies can not survive without . <p> Eventually , this operational reality will pass from de-facto practice to established convention . The global order will sacrifice its ideological claims to an open sea to save itself from absolute darkness . In doing so , it will formally codify the geographic reality on the ground , handing the sovereign keys of the strait directly to Iran and Oman . An arrangement that may well continue until such time that the world eventually returns to negotiating new norms for interdependency across both the physical and virtual spheres of influence . Some in the United States and Israel may sulk in the wake of this transformed global reality , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ for now . <h> Conclusion <p> What does this all mean for any new emergent global order ? The first shift requires abandoning the illusion that sovereignty is a universal right that can be guaranteed by any multilateral rulebook . The ' Hormuz gambit ' has demonstrated that customary international law was never a gift of reason to humanity ; it was a precedent codified by whoever held the power at the time . In a fortress world , sovereignty is no longer granted ; it is negotiated purely on the basis of leverage . <p> Just as the 1857 Sound Dues ended only when a coalition paid Copenhagen to codify its preferred rules , and just as T ? rkiye 's 1936 Montreux gambit turned geographic anxiety into lasting diplomatic leverage , Iran has asserted a new paradigm . It has shown that a physical chokepoint can neutralise a virtual financial blockade : sovereignty now belongs to the state that can make denial of its waters prohibitively costly for its adversaries . Through the siege , Iran has tested a new balance of power , and Washington 's sudden @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ The United States did not yield to legal arguments at the UN but it did so to the economic gravity of the physical siege . <p> The lesson is stark : the rules-based order is no longer enforced solely by American hegemony , but increasingly by a state 's capacity to inflict or withstand economic pain . This mutual capitulation is the modern equivalent of Montreux . It shows that custodians of the virtual order can no longer weaponise finance without risking catastrophic geographic retaliation . Ultimately , the global order must sacrifice ideological dogma to avoid systemic breakdown . By trading sanctions relief for the reopening of the Strait , the world is moving from the raw brutality of fortress siegecraft towards a negotiated interdependence that recognises and balances the hard realities of both physical geography and virtual finance . <p> What will eventually emerge is a new form of negotiated interdependence . The neo-medieval siege can not be the permanent endgame as an absolute blockade would be economically unsustainable for all actors . As the costs of the Hormuz crisis force the system to adapt , a more @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the pragmatic calculations of great powers and an emergent " cartel of the non-aligned . " Rather than import-dependent nations simply accepting Iranian regulatory taxation while the United States retreats to the margins , the more pragmatic outcome is a negotiated disarmament of competing cartazes . If and whenever the G7 framework for a 60-day final settlement succeeds -- placing the United States on a path to remove its financial blockade and sanctions in exchange for Iran keeping the Strait open -- it may well become the first codification of this new era . <h> Additional References <p> Primary Sources and Legal Instruments <p> Convention on the Territorial Sea and the Contiguous Zone . Then came tensions , sanctions , threats , strikes , and the familiar choreography of maximum pressure . <p> Then reality returned . <p> Reality has one unforgivable flaw : it does not applaud slogans . <p> A strike can damage a facility . <p> It can not @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ civilization . <p> It can not solve a geopolitical equation . <p> Sooner or later , diplomacy returns . It always does . Under another name . With another logo . Wrapped in louder language . But carrying the same old truth : even empires must negotiate . <p> Trump , of course , does not call this a return . He never retreats . He relocates the finish line . He never admits a reversal . The school of the golden megaphone . <p> He does not merely speak to the world . <p> He interrupts it . <p> Every summit becomes a stage . Every crisis becomes an episode . Every contradiction becomes a trailer for the next act . <p> His genius is real . He understood before many others that attention is the oil of the twenty-first century . Every provocation is a well . Every scandal is a pipeline . Every threat is an emotional refinery . He is the symptom of an @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ doctrine , performance competes with institutions , and volume pretends to be strength . <p> He did not create this world . <p> He mastered it . <p> This is why reducing him to a clown is lazy . A clown makes noise because he must . Trump makes noise because he knows it works . He turns outrage into currency , confusion into leverage , fatigue into submission . He has transformed politics into a casino where every contradiction is another spin of the wheel -- and the house , somehow , remains branded with his name . <p> But history is not television . <p> It does not reward only those who dominate the moment . @@138408620 <h> The Left and Breaching Capitalism 's Digital Fortress <p> The battle for socialist liberation in the twenty-first century can not be fought with the weapons of the last century . In an era in which algorithms hold sway , in which the influence of artificial intelligence over media , culture , education , and labor continues to expand , and in which economic policies and strategies are formulated on the basis of big data and algorithmic analysis , the left finds itself confronted with an existential question : how can movements that still organize themselves according to traditional logic confront a digital capitalism that has become technologically advanced to an unprecedented degree ? <p> This text is not merely a call to develop tools ; it is a call to transform organizational and intellectual consciousness toward a deep understanding of the nature of the digital battle . The gap in question is not simply a gap in ' technical mastery ' ; it is a gap in grasping that digital space has become a class battlefield in which capitalism dominates , programs , and subjugates , while the left @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ clear digital vision . Closing this gap is no longer a luxury ; it is a condition for the survival of the left itself , since today 's battle is waged in algorithms and networks just as much as it is waged on the ground . <p> The struggle over technology is not a battle against science ; it is a battle against the monopoly that dominant powers hold over it in order to boost their profits . Artificial intelligence should not be regarded as a threat in itself , but rather as a field of struggle whose features are shaped by the balance of social , political , and economic forces . Recent years have witnessed an unprecedented acceleration in the concentration of digital power within a limited number of giant corporations that control the infrastructure of artificial intelligence , cloud computing , and global data , granting them economic , political , and cultural influence that at times surpasses the influence of numerous states . <p> Technology as Capitalism 's Means of Overcoming Its Crises <p> When confronted with crises , capitalism resorts to reproducing itself through advanced @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ its exploitative core . In the 2008 crisis , technology and scientific methods were used to rescue the financial system while loading the cost of the losses onto the working classes . During the COVID-19 pandemic of 2020 , capitalism managed to overcome the crisis by reinforcing automation , artificial intelligence , and remote work , which ensured the continuity of production through new mechanisms that reduced reliance on human labor and increased corporate profits , at the cost of unstable working conditions for millions . <p> With the broad surge of artificial intelligence since 2023 , capitalism has entered a new phase of restructuring the labor market . Reliance on automation and intelligent systems has expanded across numerous sectors , and growing concerns have emerged over the future of millions of jobs , even as technology companies achieve enormous profits as a result of their monopoly over the new digital and knowledge infrastructure . <p> These policies show how capitalism benefits from science as a tool for structuring the system and ensuring its continuity . At times , it even borrows certain socialist ideas , such as state intervention @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ retreat from those gains once the crisis has passed and to reproduce exploitation through more advanced mechanisms . <p> Scientific Flexibility and the Digital Revolution as a Modern Class Struggle <p> In light of these challenges , the left must draw on scientific progress by reformulating its discourse and its tools in a scientific manner . This requires using modern tools to analyze social issues and developing a realistic discourse along with flexible organizational mechanisms capable of attracting young people who have grown up in a world dominated by technology . Investing in scientific tools does not mean identifying with capitalist values ; it is a strategy for harnessing them in the service of social justice and reducing class inequality , as a step toward building a more humane socialist system . <p> If the previous industrial revolutions transformed the equations of production through the machine and steam , then electricity , then computing , the current phase , founded on artificial intelligence , big data , and digital platforms , is reshaping production , labor , knowledge , and human communication in a manner that is more profound and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and artificial intelligence systems have become central tools for reproducing domination in relatively invisible ways , through influencing public opinion , directing individual and collective behavior , and controlling access to knowledge and information . <p> Yet most left organizations remain digitally backward , which places them in a position of weakness . This lag reflects a failure to grasp that digital development has become an existential condition for socialist struggle . The left 's lack of modern digital and knowledge tools places it in an unequal confrontation with a capitalist system that owns the global platforms , the data , and the computing and artificial intelligence infrastructure , tools that grant it an unprecedented capacity to shape consciousness and influence social and political behavior . <p> Reclaiming the Initiative <p> While the left is currently losing one of the battles because it treats technology as a secondary tool , the war has not yet been decided . Victory requires translating vision into concrete programs of action grounded in the conscious use of technology . The left can not remain in a defensive position ; it must become an active @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ integrate it into its liberatory project . <p> Even so , technology is no substitute for conscious human organization . Real power lies in organized human beings capable of harnessing these means in the service of their goals . Artificial intelligence is an effective tool for mobilization , organization , and analysis , yet it will never replace the solidarity and grassroots work that remains the primary engine of change . <p> As a left , we have historically succeeded in offering alternatives in the fields of economics , justice , and politics , yet today we face a fateful challenge : we have not yet developed a comprehensive , alternative digital vision capable of breaking capitalism 's technological grip . The most important dialectical lesson we must absorb is that technology is not a ' neutral tool ' that falls from the sky ; rather , it is a class battlefield par excellence . The fundamental problem does not lie in the essence of artificial intelligence or automation , but in the ' relations of ownership ' that govern them , that is , in the monopoly that major @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ conflict , surveil the masses , and standardize human consciousness in the service of accumulating profit . <p> On this basis , it is no longer sufficient for the left to stand in the position of ' critic ' or ' spectator , ' since it must put forward new and bold mechanisms for using technology within democratic , participatory , and transparent frameworks . We need a ' popular artificial intelligence ' that operates under societal oversight and is developed through digital cooperatives , aiming to distribute wealth and organize production in the service of genuine human needs rather than the whims of the market and the strengthening of domination and militarism . We also need open-source models , progressive digital platforms , and cooperative technological initiatives that are not subject to the logic of commercial monopoly , and that allow communities and the masses to participate in managing knowledge and data and in developing new technologies . <p> A genuine confrontation requires us to ' breach the digital fortress ' of capitalism , which means entering into the very heart of the technical process , and understanding the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ them with a liberatory orientation . Merely standing at the walls of this technology and crying out in condemnation of its exploitation will change nothing in reality and will leave the left isolated within outdated intellectual ghettos . <p> We are called upon to take possession of the tools of our age , since just as Marx and Engels transformed the economic and philosophical sciences of their time from tools that justified the existing order into a theoretical and practical weapon in the hands of the working class , the left today is called upon to be an active and programming force in this arena . We must move from the position of the ' passive user ' subject to the terms of capitalist platforms , to the position of the ' alternative producer ' who puts forward a technology that is communal , open , and liberated . <p> The struggle over artificial intelligence is no longer simply about the future of technology ; it concerns the future of labor , democracy , culture , and social justice . Without an active left presence in this field , digital @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in the service of its own interests and will continue to control the development of the human mind and the human future . <p> The true strength of the left lies in its ability to integrate grassroots human organization with digital mastery , so that digital space becomes a supportive and effective arena , not a substitute for struggle ; rather , a wing on which it can soar toward a more humane and more just socialist future . <h> Subscribe to Our Newsletter <p> Rezgar Akrawi is a leftist writer and researcher focused on technology , AI , the digital revolution , and the development of contemporary leftist thought and practice in response to these transformations . Photo courtesy of the author <p> One morning in the dead of winter , I woke up at 9 am to call my friend Ahmad to get ready . <p> We were heading to Deir al-Balah to the main office of the Social Developmental Forum ( SDF ) , where we were volunteering as part of an education advocacy campaign to push international organizations to include education within their emergency response programs in Gaza . <p> Until recently , I did not even know what an advocacy campaign was . I had certainly never imagined myself participating in one . I first learned about advocacy through a training program organized by SDF , the first training I had attended since the Israel 's genocide in Gaza began . <p> SDF is a well-known local organization recognized for amplifying the voices of youth and women by empowering them and educating them on how to play an effective role in society and participate in decision-making . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the organization shifted its focus to urgent humanitarian support for the community . Over time , however , it decided to relaunch the sixth edition of its youth program , Yalla Change , but with a completely different agenda . <p> With the absence of an effective governmental role due to the war , the growing influence of international organizations , the overwhelming scale of needs , and the shortage of helping hands , the program centered around one core idea : how ordinary young people could become agents of change . <p> Whether in your displaced persons ' camp , your neighborhood or anywhere you encounter a problem , the message was simple : be the person willing to change it . <p> By the time the program began in late September , we had already learned how to design and amplify community initiatives , advocate for social causes , and turn ideas into practical action . <p> Colors <p> Now we had reached the final stage of the program : applying what we had learned through real initiatives . Around 50 youth participated -- 30 from Gaza and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ teams of five or six members , and each team had to design its own initiative . " <p> We knew that most teams would focus on direct service problems caused by the genocide -- damaged infrastructure , shortages and emergency aid . But we wanted to move in a different direction . <p> We realized that what all of us missed most was not only safety , but Gaza itself as we once knew it : streets glowing under yellow lights at night , the blue sea , balconies filled with mint and basil plants , and the colors that once made the city feel alive instead of the endless gray of rubble . <p> We missed Gaza 's colors . <p> So our initiative aimed to create a small public space filled with life that could serve as a simple landmark and gathering point -- a place where young people could sit , talk and take photos . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ existed beyond destruction . Deir al-Balah avoided the worst of the destruction in Israel 's genocidal assault , though , after the wholesale devastation inflicted on the Gaza Strip , standards of destruction in Gaza became fundamentally different from anywhere else in the world . With over 80 percent of all buildings across Gaza damaged or destroyed in Israel 's unhinged violence since October 2023 , even the harshest living conditions begin to be viewed as a form of " relative luxury . " <p> In Deir al-Balah , some 3,500 buildings were destroyed or damaged . @@138440341 <h> Thank You , Israel , for Burning the Old Order <p> One must give credit where credit is due : Israel , by pursuing its strategy with all the delicacy of a sledgehammer in a glasshouse , has achieved what diplomats , clerics , monarchs , generals , and think-tank acrobats spent decades failing to accomplish . It has helped bury the old Sunni -- Shia melodrama as the organizing principle of West Asian politics , and it has made the American " security umbrella " look less like an umbrella than a very expensive lightning rod . <p> This is no small accomplishment . For years , the region was instructed to understand itself through sectarian grammar . Riyadh and Tehran were not merely rival capitals ; they were presented as metaphysical opposites , civilizational antagonists , eternal enemies locked in theological combat . Every battlefield was translated into sectarian prose . Yemen , Syria , Lebanon , Iraq : all were reduced to the lazy vocabulary of Sunni versus Shia , as though history itself had been outsourced to cable-news interns and intelligence cut-outs . <p> Then @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ began the correction in 2023 by brokering the Saudi-Iranian rapprochement , assisted by the quieter groundwork of Iraq and Oman . Russia , too , contributed by helping normalize the idea that regional actors could speak across blocs without first asking permission from Washington 's imperial reception desk . But Israel , with its characteristic gift for turning every tactical victory into a strategic ulcer , has completed the process . Its rampage across Gaza , Lebanon , Syria , Yemen , and Iran 's orbit has reminded the region that the primary contradiction is not sectarian identity . It is imperial architecture . It is Zionist violence . It is the American security order that protects both while charging its clients premium rates for the privilege of being endangered . <p> Whatever one thinks of Saudi Arabia , Iran , Qatar , Pakistan , Turkiye , Egypt , or any of the regimes presently rearranging the furniture of West Asia is , at this point , almost secondary . @@138447543 <h> How Subsea Cables Became Important to the World <p> Nearly 30 years after the laying of the first successful transatlantic cable in 1866 , Rudyard Kipling wrote " Let us be one ! " in a classic poem about the mysteries of deep-sea communication titled " The Deep-Sea Cables . " <p> Today , it 's been over half a century of telegraph lines having given way to fibre-optic cables , but their unifying promise remains the same . The seabed is the next great battleground , transforming into an arena of great-power competition , surveillance , and sabotage . After all , fibre-optic data cables carry 99% of global digital traffic , including military , diplomatic , government and financial communications and flows . <p> Even as trust erodes and risks grow , global cabling has become extremely critical to the world , abandoning commercial logic and rather being a mirror to geopolitical alignment . How did these cables transform into what can only be called the new arteries of power ? <h> Lay Of The Land ( Read : Sea ) <p> Submarine networks , a.k.a. subsea @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ floor to transmit data between different geographical regions . These cables are critical as they carry more than 99% of international data , unlike satellites that handle only a small percentage of global traffic . Every cable comprises strands of optical fibre that transmit data as light pulse signals , which travel at extremely high speeds . However , they weaken over long distances , leading to repeaters being fitted all along the cable for boosting signal strengths . <p> These underwater systems are connected to terrestrial networks by landing stations , thus forming a continuous global web . For instance , when a user in New Zealand accesses a server in the United States , this request travels through a number of subsea cables across the Pacific Ocean , with the physical path directly impacting latency , even after the software routing has been optimised . <h> In The Deep End : Of Chokepoints And Disruptions <p> Today , there are more than 600 subsea cables spanning a whopping 1.5 million km across the ocean floor . These cables are precision-engineered strands of steel and glass , rather than @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ laid along the routes optimised for efficiency , not survivability , and are no thicker than garden hoses , carrying around 99% of transoceanic internet traffic . They 've worked in the past because no one has tried to seriously break them , an assumption that 's now under strain . <p> In 2024 and 2025 , several undersea cables were severed by the Houthi forces which were reacting to the war in Gaza , resulting in severe internet disruptions across South Asia and the Middle East . Within minutes , the internet in multiple countries , including the UAE , Kuwait , India , and many Gulf nations went from high-speed efficiency to a snail 's pace . <p> As tensions escalated in March 2026 in the West Asia war , a consortium led by tech giant Meta announced that it was halting work on the 2Africa Pearls project in the Persian Gulf . One of the most ambitious undersea cable networks to have ever been built , the project suffered due to the Strait of Hormuz blockages , which is n't just a strategic energy corridor but also @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the Red Sea , saw a dual chokepoint for these subsea cables , which were never designed for war . <p> It 's not the only region where subsea cables are under attack . In September 2022 , the Nord Stream pipeline explosions in the Baltic Sea launched a damage investigation into the SwePol undersea cable , which passed near two of the gas leak sites arising from the explosions . Subsequent incidents drew global attention to these risks , showing how incidents from one region could possibly endanger infrastructure in another . <p> Increased submarine and vessel activity along Baltic and Atlantic routes has also increased concerns about subsea surveillance , as adversaries monitor and map critical cable routes . <p> The situation is not so different on the other side of the world in Asia . For instance , Taiwan has been reporting 7-8 cable breaks annually . In March 2025 , China revealed the existence of a powerful deep-sea cable cutter that could sever cables as deep as 13,000 ft. deep underneath the surface of the sea . That 's just under twice the current operational depth @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ -- or morbid , for that matter . For instance , in March 2024 , there were major internet outages reported across the African continent when a subsea avalanche supposedly damaged four subsea cables along the West African coastline . At that time , Google 's nearly-15,000-km-long lifeline , the Equiano undersea cable , came to the rescue , connecting Portugal to South Africa , with landing points in Togo , Nigeria , and more places along the route . <h> The Future Is Underwater <p> Interestingly , despite the ever-growing importance of undersea cables , there 's no single authority that governs this massive subsea infrastructure . Plus , the institutions and laws governing them have n't kept up with times either . For instance , the relevant provisions of the 1982 UNCLOS ( UN Convention on the Law of the Sea ) were drafted for a different age and built on conventions signed by monarchs even further back in 1884 ! <p> Even though awareness of the vulnerabilities faced by undersea infrastructure is growing , regional and national responses vary widely in scope and ambition . Ideally , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ system that links regional and national efforts with international ones and modernises the institutional and legal regime . <p> As our reliance on globally distributed workloads and real-time data increases , undersea cables will remain critical -- if anything , their role will become all the more important . With latency becoming a key metric in 2026 , especially for applications such as real-time collaboration tools , financial trading , cloud gaming , and more , the challenges -- technical , political , and territorial -- can only be overcome with the somewhat fragile cooperation of the various organisations and governments from around the world . <p> Malavika Madgula is a writer and coffee lover from Mumbai , India , with a post-graduate degree in finance and an interest in the world . @@138458488 <h> 81 years of the UN Charter : How did it come about ? <h> On June 26 , 1945 , 50 nations signed a charter meant to prevent another world war . The nations who opposed the charter eventually signed off too . Yet , the structure they built has barely changed since with the United Nations the subject of criticism in the 21st century . <p> On June 26 , 1945 , at the Veterans ' War Memorial Building in San Francisco , delegates from 50 nations signed the Charter of the United Nations ( UN ) , a document of 111 articles spread across 19 chapters , agreed upon over two months of negotiation . <p> The conference , formally called the United Nations Conference on International Organisation , convened on April 25 , while the war against Japan was still raging . Germany surrendered midway through , on May 8 . <p> The charter was unanimously adopted by a standing ovation on June 25 and formally signed the next day . The Charter signed that day had four core purposes as laid out in Article 1 @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ among nations , achieving international cooperation on economic , social , cultural , and humanitarian problems , and serving as a center for harmonising the actions of nations toward these ends . <p> What the Charter did not mention at all was equally significant there is no reference to the environment , sustainable development , climate , nuclear weapons , pandemics , or cyberwarfare . <h> The summit that built the blueprint <p> The Charter did not emerge from nowhere . Its intellectual lineage ran through a number of wartime summits and declarations . The idea of the United Nations began to be articulated in August 1941 , when Roosevelt and Churchill signed the Atlantic Charter , a joint statement of Allied war aims and principles for a post-war peaceful international order . <p> In October 1943 , the Moscow Conference , where the foreign ministers of the US , UK , USSR , and China met and issued the Moscow Declaration , marked the first firm Soviet commitment to establish a general international organisation to maintain peace and security . <p> That same November , Roosevelt and Churchill flew @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 26 , 1943 ) , a summit with China 's Chiang Kai-shek that outlined the Allied position against Japan , produced the Cairo Declaration demanding Japan 's unconditional surrender , and discussed the future of Asia . <p> Immediately after , the three leaders reconvened in Tehran for the Tehran Conference ( November 28 -- December 1 , 1943 ) , the first time the Big Three had all met together , where Roosevelt more or less convinced Stalin and Churchill to endorse some kind of peacekeeping international organisation , a successor to the League of Nations . <p> In the month after the Bretton Woods Conference , representatives of the US , USSR , UK , and China met in Washington for the Dumbarton Oaks conversations for proposals for an organisation to be called " The United Nations , " built on the sovereign equality of states , with a General Assembly , Security Council , and Secretariat , though leaving the critical question of Security Council voting procedure unresolved . <p> That gap was closed at the Yalta Conference in February 1945 , where the Big Three settled @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to this day . <p> Story continues below this ad <p> The four sponsoring governments , the US , UK , USSR , and China , then invited nations that had declared war on Germany or Japan to San Francisco . Fifty nations attended ; Poland , an original signatory to the 1942 declaration , missed the conference and signed later as the 51st original member . <p> The United Nations formally came into existence on October 24 , 1945 , now observed as United Nations Day , when the five permanent members and a majority of the other signatories ratified the Charter . <p> Under Articles 53 and 107 , later known as the " Enemy State Clauses , " Germany , Italy , and Japan were designated enemy states . In legal terms , any UN member could take military action against them without Security Council authorisation . <p> The three principal Axis powers had no role in drafting the document that would govern the post-war world order . Italy had invaded Ethiopia in 1935 , Japan had seized Manchuria in 1931 and invaded China in 1937 , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ sequence of aggressions that had destroyed the League of Nations and precipitated the war in the first place . <p> From enemy states to member states <p> Story continues below this ad <p> The path into the UN was not simple for the Axis powers . Italy was admitted to the UN on December 14 , 1955 , as part of a " package deal " in which the Security Council recommended sixteen countries for admission simultaneously , a compromise between the Western powers and the Soviet Union that had used its veto to block admission of nations it regarded as aligned with the West . <p> Japan 's admission took longer . The Soviet Union blocked Japan 's membership through the early 1950s . It was only after Tokyo and Moscow established diplomatic relations in late 1956 , with the USSR explicitly agreeing to support Japan 's UN membership bid , that Japan was admitted on December 18 , 1956 , as the 80th member of the United Nations , eleven years after the organisation 's founding . <p> The Soviet Union viewed the Federal Republic of Germany as @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ image , the US , UK , and France would never allow the Soviet-backed German Democratic Republic to join . Each of the two Germanys was , from the other side 's perspective , simply illegitimate . <p> Both the Federal Republic of Germany and the German Democratic Republic were admitted simultaneously on September 18 , 1973 . <p> Story continues below this ad <h> The growing irrelevance and reform question <p> The wars in Gaza and Ukraine have put the UN 's central promise of collective security under its most visible strain in decades . A permanent Security Council member invaded Ukraine , and Gaza has seen mass civilian casualties . In 2024 alone , seven draft resolutions failed due to a veto , the highest number since 1986 , with the US casting three vetoes on Gaza , and Russia four across Gaza , Ukraine , Sudan , and outer space . <p> Analysts and member states increasingly describe the organisation as having lost credibility as an enforcer of the very Charter it was built to uphold . UN Secretary-General Ant ? nio Guterres has described the Security @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ system " that " does n't correspond to the world of today , " adding that it has " systematically failed " to end the most dramatic conflicts the world faces , such as those in Sudan , Gaza , and Ukraine . <p> The Security Council veto , intended as a mechanism to bind the great powers into the system , became a tool of paralysis . Since 1945 , the veto has been exercised almost 300 times . The Security Council 's non-permanent membership was expanded from 6 to 10 seats in 1963 , the only structural change to the Council since its founding . <p> The five permanent members have not changed in over eight decades , a composition now widely criticised as a relic of 1945 power realities that bears no relation to today 's global demographics , economies , or geopolitical weight . <p> Story continues below this ad <p> India has made its case for a permanent seat on the grounds of size , contribution , and democratic legitimacy . India has been elected to the Security Council eight times as a non-permanent member @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ argues that the G4 , a Council designed over 80 years ago , no longer reflects contemporary realities . <p> India 's case rests on its standing as the world 's most populous country , its historic contributions to the UN system , and its leadership among developing nations . Four of the five permanent members have expressed support ; China remains the sole P5 member opposed . The debate over a permanent seat , however , is only one dimension of a deeper problem . <p> The Charter 's text has never been amended to include any of these issues : the environment , climate , pandemics , or cyberwarfare . Most of the existential challenges now dominating the global agenda , such as the climate crisis , pandemics , mass migration , and nuclear proliferation , were unimaginable in the aftermath of a catastrophic world war . <p> The UN has responded not by rewriting its founding document but by layering treaties and specialised bodies around it .

@@138471661 <h> Remembering Carlo Ginzburg , and the Shame he left us to Carry <p> On June 17th , the historian Carlo Ginzburg died in Bologna at the age of eighty-seven . For sixty years he asserted that the tiniest discarded fact , a heretical miller 's testimony , a peasant 's dream of wrestling witches , a line in an Inquisition transcript that no one else cared to read twice , could overturn what power had decided history should say . His father , Leone Ginzburg , was an anti-fascist intellectual who was tortured to death by the Nazis when Carlo was five years old . He was the son of the novelist Natalia Ginzburg . In other words , he grew up knowing just what a state can do to people who wo n't look away . This is probably why the provocative essay of his that I kept returning to , ' Bond of Shame ' , was n't about heretics or witches at all . It is an eight-page essay , published for the first time in 2010 as a chapter in a German volume ( Passionen @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ history of emotion , and republished again in 2019 in an Italian book , Il vincolo della vergogna . Letture oblique ( The Bond of Shame : Oblique Readings ) . That same year it appeared in New Left Review , and it opens with a sentence so plain you almost miss how much weight it is carrying : " The country one belongs to is not , as the usual rhetoric goes , the one you love but the one you are ashamed of . Shame can be a stronger bond than love . " 1 Shame is the emotion we are taught to be ashamed of feeling , the thing nationalists of every flag have always treated as the symptom of a traitor 's heart . Ginzburg 's whole point was that it 's the opposite . He traces it through the Iliad , where soldiers shout the word aidos at each other to keep anyone from running , shame as the glue that holds a unit together , not the thing that breaks it . He traces it through an Athenian orator 's memory of decent citizens @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . And he ends with Primo Levi , who wrote that the shame he felt in front of the Red Army soldiers who liberated Auschwitz was a shame the camp 's architects had never once felt in their lives ; proof , Levi thought , that he still belonged to something they had stepped outside of . <p> I do n't think I would have read that essay the same way a year ago . I read it this month thinking about a blind woman name Safalta Kartik in Jabalpur , assaulted inside church on 20 December 2025 by a man who holds elected office , while the people around her filmed it instead of stopping it. 2 I read it thinking about a four-hundred-year-old mosque in Ahmedabad , knocked down under the bureaucratic alibi of " road-widening , " and about the small towns in Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh and Haryana where bulldozers now arrive at a Muslim family 's door within hours of an accusation nobody has had to prove in court . Twenty-seven Muslims and one Dalit migrant were killed by vigilante mobs last year. 3 @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ against their communities in the same year , more than five times what they were counting the year this government first came to power. 4 None of this requires me to tell you what to feel about it . It only requires you to notice what it does to a country 's idea of itself . <p> What it has done , mostly , is teach people not to say it out loud . Umar Khalid has been in Tihar Jail for over five years without a trial , because he helped organize a protest against a law his government wanted unprotested . Khurram Parvez , who lost a leg to a landmine documenting Kashmir 's disappeared , was finally granted bail this month after four years inside on terror-financing charges that have produced no conviction , only headlines . Irfan Mehraj , a Kashmiri journalist , has been in prison for 1,186 days . No trial . No conviction . Only the accusation , and the waiting. 5 Twenty-two thousand civil society organizations have lost the licenses that let them receive foreign funding , most of them the ones @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to say , the ones whose job was to notice things like Jabalpur and Ahmedabad and write them down. 6 A press freedom index that ranked the country 140th a decade ago now puts it at 157th out of 180. 7 That 's not a coincidence of measurement . It 's what happens when the cheapest way to make a problem disappear is to make the person describing it sound like the problem . <p> This is the part where Ginzburg 's small , strange essay stops being literary history and starts being a key . The word for what 's happened to people like Khalid , Irfan Mehraj and Parvez is " anti-national " , the accusation that their criticism of the state is , somehow , an attack on the country itself . But the entire architecture of Ginzburg 's argument runs the other direction : the capacity to be ashamed of your country is one of the deepest proofs you have never left it . The student who gets arrested for organizing a protest is not rejecting the nation . He is doing , almost exactly , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ registering , on behalf of something bigger than himself , that a disgrace has occurred and that he is still close enough to it to feel the weight of it . You do n't prosecute that reflex because it threatens the country . You prosecute it because it 's inconvenient to the people currently running it , which are not the same thing , however often the two get described as identical . <p> There 's a structural reason this should worry people who do n't think of themselves as critics of anything . Shame , in the anthropological tradition Ginzburg is drawing on , is n't a private feeling , it needs witnesses . It needs a court willing to rule against the powerful occasionally , a press with something left to lose by lying , a watchdog nobody 's managed to buy yet . Spend a decade hollowing those things out , courts that no longer reliably check the executive , a television landscape that functions more like a megaphone than a mirror , and you have n't just made criticism harder to hear . You 've taken @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ feel ashamed of itself in the first place . What 's left in its place is n't pride . It 's just the absence of an audience . <p> The same reflex shows up at the border . India abstained , last June , on a UN resolution calling for an immediate ceasefire in Gaza , one of only two countries in Asia not to vote yes , six months after voting for almost the same resolution , 8 the contradiction explained away with language vague enough to mean whatever the moment required . The decade spent building a foothold at Iran 's Chabahar Port was allowed to wither this spring rather than risk a single phone call from Washington going badly , and even members of the opposition , not usually eager to hand the government a foreign-policy win , found themselves asking how much longer the country intends to let someone else 's capital write its own . A government that has spent ten years treating shame as a domestic threat does n't , it turns out , have much capacity left over to feel any of it @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the other side of this , because pretending it does n't exist would be its own kind of dishonesty . The government 's defenders have real arguments : three election victories , fairly won , are not nothing . Anti-terror law and demolition drives are described , by the people enforcing them , as responses to lawlessness rather than campaigns against any single community , and that defense deserves to be tested rather than dismissed . The international indexes carry their own institutional histories and blind spots . Strategic restraint over Gaza and a quiet retreat from Tehran can both be described , honestly , as the discipline of a country trying to keep its options open in a dangerous neighborhood . None of that is nothing . What it ca n't do is make the underlying habit disappear , the habit of answering every account of harm with a question about the patriotism of whoever is telling it , instead of the truth of what they 're telling . <p> Near the end of his essay , Ginzburg returns one last time to Primo Levi , to the idea @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to the people who witness an injustice and discover they were powerless to stop it , ashamed simply because they belong to the species capable of producing it in the first place . That feeling does n't check passports . It does n't evaporate because a government has decided , by decree or by habit , to call it disloyalty instead . <p> India is still , for what it 's worth , a country whose courts occasionally rule against the state , whose smaller papers still occasionally print what they 're not supposed to , whose streets still occasionally fill with more people than a government can comfortably ignore . Nobody loses a democracy in a single afternoon . It happens one citizen at a time , each one deciding , on some unremarkable Tuesday , that it 's easier this week not to look . If Carlo Ginzburg left anything behind worth keeping , it might be the reminder that looking away has never actually been the patriot 's privilege . It 's the one thing patriotism has never been able to survive . <h> Subscribe to Our @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of the Government Degree Colleges of Jammu and Kashmir . @@138511643 <p> More than 266 million people -- roughly the population of a large country -- are facing high levels of acute food insecurity across 47 countries , according to the Global Report on Food Crises 2026 ( GRFC 2026 ) report released in April this year . <p> Global acute hunger has nearly doubled over the past decade and shows no sign of retreating . In fact , two famines were declared last year -- in Gaza and parts of Sudan -- marking the first time in the report 's history that famine was declared in more than one country in the same year . <p> The scale underscores how deeply entrenched acute food insecurity and malnutrition is , but the crisis has increasingly been concentrated in a core group of countries . <p> These stark numbers are likely to shape debates at the Hamburg Sustainability Conference ( HSC 2026 ) , opening June 29 in Hamburg , Germany . With just a few years left to meet the 2030 deadline on the Sustainable Development Goals ( SDGs ) , the GRFC data presents an uncomfortable reckoning for the heads @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ : on SDG 2 ( Zero Hunger ) , the world is not moving in the right direction . <p> The report was released on April 24 , 2026 , by the United Nations ( UN ) ; the European Union ; Ministry of Economic Cooperation and Development , Germany ; the UK Foreign , Commonwealth &amp; Development Office ; the Government of Ireland ; the Group of Seven Plus and governmental and non-governmental agencies working together to address food crises . <p> In its 10th edition , the report found that 22.9 per cent of the analysed population across 47 countries ( about 266 million people ) experienced high levels of acute food insecurity in 2025 , a marginal increase from 2024 . <p> While the headline figure appears broadly stable , the report cautions that this is largely due to a reduced number of countries assessed this year rather than any meaningful improvement in conditions . The share of people facing acute hunger has remained above 20 per cent since 2020 and is nearly double what it was in 2016 . <p> The crisis was found to be @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , Bangladesh , the Democratic Republic of the Congo , Myanmar , Nigeria , Pakistan , South Sudan , Sudan , Syrian Arab Republic and Yemen -- accounted for two-thirds of all people facing high levels of acute hunger . Afghanistan , South Sudan , Sudan , and Yemen experienced the largest food crisis both in terms of the share and absolute number of people affected . <p> At the extreme end , 1.4 million people across six countries were classified under ' Catastrophe ' category -- the most severe form of acute food insecurity phase -- representing an increase of more than nine times since 2016 . As per the definition by Food and Agriculture Organization ( FAO ) of the UN , under this phase , households have an extreme lack of food and/or can not meet other basic needs even after full employment of coping strategies and starvation , death , destitution and extremely critical acute malnutrition levels are evident . <p> A further 39 million people in 32 countries were classified as being in ' Emergency ' , the second-most severe category . <p> In 2025 @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ nearly 10 million suffering from severe acute malnutrition . In addition , forced displacement continued to exacerbate food insecurity . <h> Conflict primary driver , overtakes extreme weather events <p> Conflict and insecurity were the primary drivers of acute food insecurity , overtaking extreme weather events , which had long been a leading cause . In 2025 , 19 countries where conflict was the primary driver accounted for 56 per cent of the population facing high levels of acute food insecurity , with 147.4 million people affected . This is an increase from 139.8 million in 2024 and more than double the 73.9 million recorded in 2018 . <p> " Conflict remains the primary driver of acute food insecurity and malnutrition for millions around the world , with outright famine emerging in two conflict-affected areas in the same year -- an unprecedented development , " said UN Secretary-General Ant ? nio Guterres in the foreword to the report . <p> Meanwhile , the role of weather extremes , while still significant , has relatively diminished . In 2025 , 16 countries where extreme weather was the primary driver accounted for @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ people -- down from a peak of 96.6 million in 2024 . <p> The shift is significant . For years , climate shocks such as droughts , floods , and erratic seasons had been the dominant force pushing populations into hunger . That conflict has now surpassed extreme weather as the leading driver reflects the toll of prolonged wars and instability , particularly across parts of Africa and West Asia , where fighting has simultaneously destroyed livelihoods , disrupted food systems and cut off humanitarian aid access . <h> Funding cuts threaten response <p> Compounding the crises is a sharp decline in the money available to address it . Humanitarian and development financing for food sectors in food crisis contexts has fallen back to levels last seen in 2016-2017 , nearly a decade ago , even as acute food insecurity has remained stubbornly high . The funding retreat is already limiting the ability of governments and humanitarian agencies to respond effectively , the report warns . <p> The 2026 edition of the report features the lowest country coverage in its ten-year history , with 18 countries and territories unable to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . Five of those countries -- Burkina Faso , the Republic of the Congo , Ethiopia , and displaced populations in Algeria and Ecuador -- had data available last year , representing more than 27 million people facing high levels of acute food insecurity in 2024 , but no updated estimates could be produced for 2025 . <p> The consequences are visible in the volume of data collected . The World Food Programme ( WFP ) , one of the principal data providers , conducted 800,000 survey interviews in 2025 -- a 30 per cent drop from 1.1 million the previous year -- and a further reduction is expected in 2026 . <p> Similarly , the FAO reduced its household survey interviews by around 31 per cent , from roughly 170,000 in 2024 to 118,000 in 2025 . Population coverage of food security analyses declined by about 40 per cent in Zambia , 17 per cent in Malawi , and 14 per cent in Guinea . <p> As a result , the integrity of data systems underpinning the global hunger assessment is increasingly at risk , the report warned , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ crisis that is already only partially visible . <p> As world leaders head to Hamburg , the GRFC 2026 serves as an urgent reminder that sustainability commitments must translate into essential work of funding , monitoring and responding to food crises -- before the window to act closes . 
@@138519559 <h> The Ugly Face of Israel in Gaza and Lebanon : Killing and Destruction of Human Lives as a Clear Violation of International Law <p> The ongoing Israeli military operations in Gaza and Lebanon , despite the signature on the MoU , represent one of the gravest humanitarian and legal crises of the twenty-first century . While Israel continues to justify its actions under the doctrine of self-defence following the October 2023 attacks , the scale of civilian casualties , widespread destruction of civilian infrastructure , forced displacement , restrictions on humanitarian aid , and repeated attacks on residential areas have generated unprecedented criticism from international legal scholars , human rights organisations , United Nations agencies , and international courts . The central question is no longer whether Israel possesses the right to defend itself against armed attacks ; rather , it is whether its methods of warfare have violated the principles of distinction , proportionality , necessity , and humanity that form the foundation of international humanitarian law . <p> The Human Cost of the Gaza War <p> The magnitude of destruction in Gaza has reached historic proportions . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 2023 , more than 72,000 Palestinians have died and over 172,000 have sustained injuries . A significant proportion of the dead are women and children . The destruction extends beyond human casualties to the systematic devastation of civilian infrastructure . More than 371,000 housing units have been damaged or destroyed , over half of Gaza 's hospitals are non-functional , and nearly every school has suffered destruction or severe damage . The United Nations estimates that Gaza 's human development indicators have been pushed back by approximately 77 years , requiring over $71 billion for reconstruction over the next decade . Illnesses intensified , while large portions of the country 's already fragile economy have been further crippled . <p> Extensive aid restrictions significantly worsened civilian suffering and contributed to the collapse of essential services . This situation includes the deliberate infliction of conditions that are incompatible with civilian survival ; other armed groups discriminate between combatants and civilians . The report has documented evidence that raises serious concerns regarding violations of international humanitarian law , including disproportionate attacks , collective punishment , forced displacement , and possible war crimes @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to distinguish between documented facts , legal allegations , and contested claims . Many international organisations , legal scholars , and human rights groups have argued that Israeli military actions raise serious concerns under international humanitarian law , while Israel maintains that its operations are lawful acts of self-defence against armed groups such as Hamas and Hezbollah . The following continuation presents a critical academic analysis of those allegations . <p> Destruction of Civilian Infrastructure and Collective Punishment <p> The unprecedented destruction of civilian infrastructure is one of the most controversial aspects of Israeli military operations in Gaza . International humanitarian law , particularly the Fourth Geneva Convention , requires parties to a conflict to distinguish between military objectives and civilian objects . However , satellite imagery and United Nations assessments indicate that large portions of Gaza 's urban infrastructure have been reduced to rubble . Residential neighbourhoods , universities , schools , hospitals , water facilities , bakeries , refugee camps , and municipal buildings have all suffered extensive damage . The scale of destruction has led many legal scholars to question whether the military objectives pursued by Israel @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ proportionality requires that anticipated civilian losses must not be excessive in relation to the expected military advantage . Critics argue that repeated strikes on densely populated civilian areas demonstrate a pattern inconsistent with this principle . The destruction of entire neighbourhoods has left millions dependent on humanitarian assistance and rendered vast portions of Gaza uninhabitable . <p> Furthermore , restrictions on fuel , electricity , food supplies , and humanitarian access have generated accusations of collective punishment . Article 33 of the Fourth Geneva Convention explicitly prohibits collective penalties against civilian populations . Human rights organisations have argued that depriving civilians of essential services because of the actions of armed groups constitutes collective punishment under international law . The humanitarian consequences have been severe , with widespread malnutrition , disease outbreaks , and growing risks of famine . <p> Attacks on Healthcare Facilities <p> Among the most disturbing features of the conflict has been the repeated targeting or damaging of healthcare facilities . Hospitals enjoy special protection under international humanitarian law unless they are being used for military purposes . Israeli authorities have argued that Hamas used hospitals and medical @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ centres . However , many international observers have argued that the evidence presented has often been insufficient to justify the scale of military actions undertaken . <p> The destruction of healthcare infrastructure has had devastating consequences . Thousands of wounded civilians have faced severe shortages of medicine , surgical equipment , and medical personnel . The collapse of healthcare services has turned once-manageable chronic diseases into life-threatening conditions . According to humanitarian assessments , many patients requiring cancer treatment , dialysis , or intensive care have been unable to access necessary medical support . The long-term implications extend far beyond immediate casualties . The collapse of healthcare systems creates generational consequences , increasing infant mortality , reducing life expectancy , and undermining public health for years after hostilities cease . <p> The Lebanon Front : Expansion of the Humanitarian Crisis <p> The conflict 's expansion into Lebanon has intensified concerns regarding regional stability and civilian protection . Israeli operations targeting Hezbollah positions in southern Lebanon have resulted in significant civilian displacement and infrastructure damage . Lebanese villages near the border have experienced repeated bombardments , forcing tens of thousands of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ activities undoubtedly create security concerns for Israel , critics argue that the scale of destruction in civilian areas reflects broader patterns observed in Gaza . Roads , agricultural land , schools , and public infrastructure have suffered extensive damage . Lebanon was already facing one of the world 's worst economic crises before the conflict escalated . Additional military destruction has deepened poverty , unemployment , and social instability . The humanitarian impact extends beyond immediate casualties . Educational disruptions , economic collapse , and displacement have created long-term challenges for Lebanese society . The destruction of livelihoods in agriculture and local commerce has further undermined already fragile communities . <p> International Courts and Legal Scrutiny <p> The legal scrutiny facing Israel today is unprecedented in its history . Proceedings before the International Court of Justice and investigations by the International Criminal Court have brought international humanitarian law to the centre of the global debate . The ICJ 's provisional measures orders emphasise the obligation to prevent acts prohibited under international law and to ensure humanitarian assistance reaches affected populations . Although provisional measures do not constitute a final determination @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ situation . Simultaneously , the ICC 's investigations into alleged war crimes by multiple parties , including Israeli officials and Palestinian armed groups , demonstrate that accountability questions are becoming increasingly internationalised . The legal significance of these proceedings extends beyond the current conflict because they may influence future interpretations of civilian protection during urban warfare . <p> The Crisis of Western Double Standards <p> A major theme in academic criticism concerns perceived inconsistencies in the international response . Many scholars argue that Western governments have applied international law selectively . Strategic allies often receive different treatment for actions that adversaries condemn . This perception has significantly damaged the credibility of the rules-based international order . Across Asia , Africa , Latin America , and the Middle East , many observers view Western responses to Gaza and Lebanon as evidence of double standards . The resulting erosion of trust has weakened international institutions and reduced confidence in the impartial application of international law . Critics contend that international norms lose legitimacy when enforcement appears politically selective . If accountability depends on geopolitical alignment rather than legal principles , the authority @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Moral and Political Consequences <p> Beyond legal considerations lies a profound moral question . Military superiority does not automatically confer moral legitimacy . States possess legitimate security concerns , but they also carry responsibilities toward civilian populations . The overwhelming asymmetry in military capabilities between Israel and its adversaries has intensified scrutiny of Israeli actions . History demonstrates that military victories alone usually fail to produce lasting peace . The destruction of homes , schools , hospitals , and civilian infrastructure may weaken armed organisations temporarily , but it can also generate resentment , trauma , and future cycles of conflict . Entire generations of Palestinian and Lebanese children are growing up amid war , displacement , and insecurity . The social consequences of prolonged conflict are difficult to quantify but potentially immense . Psychological trauma , educational disruption , economic collapse , and social fragmentation may persist long after military operations end . <p> Conclusion <p> From a critical academic perspective , the Israeli campaigns in Gaza and Lebanon represent one of the most controversial military operations of the modern era . Allegations of disproportionate force , collective punishment @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , and large-scale civilian casualties have generated intense international scrutiny . While Israel argues that its actions are necessary responses to security threats posed by Hamas and Hezbollah , critics contend that the scale of destruction raises fundamental questions about compliance with international humanitarian law . Future investigations , court proceedings , historical analysis , and political developments will shape the ultimate judgement . However , the immense human suffering witnessed in Gaza and Lebanon has already become a defining issue in contemporary debates over war , accountability , human rights , and the future credibility of the international legal order . <h> Related Posts <p> Gaza ( QNN ) - Israel has intensified its attacks on the Gaza Strip , killing several Palestinians , including two siblings , amid ongoing violations of the so-called US-backed ceasefire agreement .
