@@138519578 <h> When Law Becomes a Weapon : What the World Can Still Do for Palestine <p> " Arab peoples want the liberation of Palestine . Their governments want the stability of their thrones . These two ambitions are structurally incompatible . That is the real conflict -- and it runs deeper , and older , than anything Israel has ever done to its neighbors . " <p> The Myth of Unity <p> There is a persistent fiction in Arab political discourse and in much of Western analysis : the idea of a potentially united Arab world that chooses not to act for Palestine . As though passivity were a reversible decision -- a switch that just needs the right hand to flip it . <p> Arab regimes have not simply chosen not to act for Palestine . Over decades , they have constructed architectures of interest in which any meaningful action on Palestine 's behalf directly threatens their own political survival . Passivity is not a choice made in the moment -- it is the output of a system . <p> Since the Nakba of 1948 , three major military @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 1967 , 1973 . But the 1967 defeat -- by its totality and its speed -- produced a lasting political effect that historiography has consistently underestimated : it shattered the Nasserist project of Arab unity as a shared horizon , and left in its place nation-states that have progressively made regime survival their primary foreign policy doctrine . <p> What exists in its place -- a mosaic of regimes with contested legitimacies , dependent economies , and armies frequently bound by defense agreements to external powers -- does not constitute a collective actor . It is an archipelago of individual calculations . <p> The Geography of Interests <p> Egypt is analytically the most instructive case . The first Arab state to sign a peace treaty with Israel -- the Camp David Accords in 1979 -- Cairo has since received annual US military aid documented at approximately $1.3 billion per year by the Congressional Research Service . Breaking with Israel would mean breaking with Washington , which underwrites the Egyptian military apparatus -- itself the central pillar of regime stability since 2013 . This dependence is not a betrayal in any @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Jordan faces a structurally comparable situation . The UNHCR estimates that more than two million Palestinian refugees and their descendants hold Jordanian citizenship . The 1994 Wadi Araba peace treaty formalized a security relationship including intelligence cooperation documented by historian Avi Shlaim and multiple journalistic sources . Any large-scale popular mobilization on the Palestinian question carries a destabilization risk the Hashemite monarchy weighs with extreme caution . <p> The Gulf monarchies present the most paradoxical configuration . The UAE and Bahrain formalized normalization under the Abraham Accords in September 2020 . Morocco followed in December 2020 , exchanging normalization for US recognition of its sovereignty over Western Sahara . Saudi Arabia had not formalized normalization , but discussions were well advanced before October 2023 , according to the Wall Street Journal , the Financial Times , and the Washington Institute for Near East Policy . The suspension since then is characterized by most analysts as a tactical recalibration -- not an ideological rupture . <p> The conclusion is analytical , not moral : the structural interests of these regimes converge , to varying degrees , around a regional status quo @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ but never resolved . <p> Peoples Against Their States <p> Against this geography of official interests , public opinion data paint a radically different picture . <p> The Arab Opinion Index ( Arab Center for Research and Policy Studies , Doha ) , conducted in 2023 among more than 33,000 respondents in seventeen Arab countries , found that more than 90% oppose their government recognizing Israel -- a figure stable across several years of tracking , though polling in authoritarian contexts requires appropriate methodological caution . A Zogby International survey in six Arab countries in 2022 confirms that Palestinian solidarity remains the foreign policy question on which Arab public opinion shows the strongest consensus and the widest gap with government positions . <p> This gap is not a passing anomaly . In non-democratic regimes , public opinion is a variable to be managed , not a constraint to be answered . Pro-Palestinian rhetoric in official Arab media functions as an emotional pressure valve -- permitting symbolic solidarity that never translates into political pressure on governments . <p> The architecture has one structural limit , identified by Princeton political scientist Amaney @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ authoritarian regimes , because they can transform into mobilizations against corruption and internal inequality . Several Arab governments have restricted pro-Palestinian demonstrations since October 2023 -- not out of sympathy for Israel , but out of fear of their own populations . <p> The central paradox : the Palestinian cause is the most broadly supported cause in the Arab world at the popular level , and the most comprehensively abandoned at the state level . This gap is not a coincidence . It is a deliberate political construction . <p> What Israel Understood <p> Israeli regional policy since the 1970s has rested on a lucid reading of this reality . Strategic doctrine -- articulated in Oded Yinon 's 1982 analysis published in the journal Kivunim and documented in the work of historians Benny Morris , Avi Shlaim , and Rashid Khalidi -- postulates that Arab fragmentation favors Israeli security , and that moderate Arab regimes bound to Washington constitute de facto partners in managing the Palestinian question . <p> Conventional military superiority . Israel maintains a significant technological advantage over all its neighbors -- sustained by a defense budget at @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ unmatched American technology transfers . This advantage remains real . But Gaza has exposed a documented limit : technological superiority does not guarantee strategic victory in high-intensity urban asymmetric warfare . The cost-result ratio of the Gaza operation , analyzed by researchers at the International Institute for Strategic Studies ( IISS ) , now fuels internal debates within Israel itself . <p> Unconditional American support . The United States has provided Israel more than $158 billion in assistance since 1948 -- the bulk military aid since 1973 ( Congressional Research Service ) . This relationship remains structurally robust . But the Gallup poll of March 2024 recorded for the first time a majority of American Democrats disapproving of Israel 's military conduct in Gaza -- pointing to a generational transformation of the coalitions that have sustained this relationship . The trajectory is documented and its direction is unambiguous . <p> Impunity in international legal forums . This is the pillar showing the most measurable fracture . The ICJ , in its order of January 26 , 2024 , found that South Africa 's genocide claims were " plausible " and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ merits . In November 2024 , the ICC Pre-Trial Chamber issued arrest warrants for Prime Minister Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity . The practical effects on their international mobility are already documented . <p> Five Real Levers <p> The solutions conventionally advanced -- peace process negotiations , two-state conferences , international summits -- have demonstrated their structural limits over decades . They presuppose a balance of parties and a mutual good faith that documented facts do not permit establishing . What follows proposes levers resting not on assumptions of goodwill , but on verifiable mechanisms of constraint and established historical precedent . <p> Cut off the weapons . SIPRI data establish that between 2019 and 2023 , the United States accounted for 69% of Israeli arms imports . Germany ranks second : according to the Bundesministerium f ? r Wirtschaft und Klimaschutz , German military export licenses to Israel rose from ? 32.4 million in 2022 to ? 326.5 million in 2023 -- a tenfold increase in twelve months . Italy suspended new arms export licenses in April 2024 under @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ July 2024 that the government had failed to properly assess the risk of British weapons being used in violation of international humanitarian law , leading to partial license suspension in September 2024 . Arms transfer conditionality is not a theoretical option : it is an operational mechanism already activated under judicial and parliamentary pressure in multiple European democracies . Gulf Cooperation Council states , with a combined GDP of approximately $2.1 trillion ( IMF , 2024 ) , hold a substantial complementary lever -- untapped for want of coordinated political will . <p> Prosecute without pause . The ICC arrest warrants of November 2024 impose an immediately operational travel restriction across 124 member states . Any visit by Netanyahu to a member state would trigger an obligation to arrest . Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese 's March 2024 report characterizes Israeli acts in Gaza as genocide within the meaning of the 1948 Convention , contributing to the documentary corpus of ongoing proceedings . The strategy : feed and systematize these procedures through independent fact documentation , additional state interventions , and expert reports mandated by UN bodies . <p> Suspend the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ interest calculations : for the UAE , access to the F-35 and security cover against Iran ; for Bahrain , an analogous security alignment ; for Morocco , recognition of its sovereignty over Western Sahara . None of these agreements contains a binding clause linked to Israeli conduct in the West Bank or Gaza . Their formal suspension is technically possible at any time . Turkey has traced the path : bilateral trade suspended in May 2024 , participation in ICC proceedings , intervention before the ICJ in support of South Africa . This model is replicable . <p> Rebuild a Palestinian voice . Any external pressure strategy is structurally limited without a credible Palestinian interlocutor . The Palestinian Authority registers approval ratings below 30% in Gaza ( Palestinian Center for Policy and Survey Research ) . Hamas faces military fragility and diplomatic isolation . The emergence of a third pole of representation -- rooted in civil society , carried by lawyers , intellectuals , local officials , and figures of unarmed resistance -- is a strategic necessity . The global Palestinian diaspora , estimated at more than 14 million @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , and financial resource still largely unmobilized . <p> Mobilize Western civil societies . In democratic systems , foreign policy is ultimately constrained by domestic electoral balances . A YouGov poll in March 2024 across six European countries found majorities favoring restrictions on arms sales to Israel . The March 2024 Gallup poll recorded the first plurality of Americans disapproving of Israeli military conduct in Gaza in decades . The BDS campaign , active since 2005 , has produced documented results in academic and cultural domains ; its targeted extension to the arms industry applies the model to a lever of higher impact . <p> What Law Permits and Politics Refuses <p> The disarmament of Israel -- including its nuclear arsenal -- is the question that international diplomacy systematically refuses to raise . It must be raised , with precision . <p> Israel is not a signatory to the NPT . It has concluded no comprehensive safeguards agreement with the IAEA . Its nuclear installations -- notably the Dimona complex -- have never been subjected to binding international inspection . These facts are uncontested and appear in annual IAEA reports @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ estimates Israel 's operational stockpile at approximately 90 warheads as of 2023 . <p> This situation was formalized during Nixon-Meir discussions in 1969 -- partially declassified and documented by Avner Cohen in Israel and the Bomb ( Columbia University Press , 1998 ) . The Neither Confirm Nor Deny ( NCND ) doctrine allowed Israel to develop nuclear capabilities without facing the diplomatic pressure or sanctions applied to other states in comparable situations . <p> The asymmetry is stark : Israel benefits from de facto nuclear immunity ; Iran has been subjected to some of the most severe sanctions in recent diplomatic history for a program whose military dimensions remain unestablished by IAEA inspectors . International law scholars John Quigley ( Ohio State University ) and Richard Falk ( Princeton University ) have characterized this asymmetry as incompatible with the sovereign equality principle of Article 2 of the UN Charter . <p> A legally grounded disarmament strategy requires three simultaneous tracks : universalization of the NPT as a condition of any commercial or security agreement with Israel ; formal reopening of the Middle East Weapons of Mass Destruction Free Zone @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Review Conference , reaffirmed in 2000 and 2010 , systematically blocked by the US-Israeli veto ; and application of Article 51 of Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions as conditionality on conventional weapons transfers . None of these mechanisms requires new law . What they lack is not a legal foundation . It is the political will to apply them without exception . <p> The Global South Rises <p> The most geopolitically significant development of 2023 -- 2026 is neither military nor diplomatic in the classical sense . It is a mutation in the structure of international legitimacy -- of which Gaza is simultaneously the trigger and the symptom . <p> South Africa 's ICJ referral in December 2023 marks a qualitative rupture . For the first time , it was not an Arab country but a Southern African nation -- carrying its own experience of apartheid -- that brought the world 's highest court into a genocide case . Thirteen states have since filed declarations of intervention , including Bolivia , Colombia , Mexico , Ireland , Nicaragua , Turkey , and Malaysia -- a geography that transcends @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the Palestinian cause -- from an Arab or Islamic cause to a universal cause of international law -- is strategically decisive . When Ireland , Bolivia , and South Africa jointly carry a proceeding before the ICJ , the interpretive frame of the " Israeli-Arab conflict " or " clash of civilizations " becomes analytically inoperative . <p> This reflects a broader recomposition : the emergence of a Global South that no longer recognizes itself in an international order built on power relations inherited from incomplete decolonization , and that mobilizes the legal instruments of that order against its own contradictions . Palestine is the most visible case of a dynamic equally touching the regime of unilateral sanctions , IMF and World Bank voting structures , trade rules , and UN Security Council reform . <p> A World Order on Trial <p> There is no quick solution to what decades of occupation , colonial expansion , and mass violence have produced in Palestine , Gaza , and Lebanon . Any promise of rapid resolution would be analytically dishonest . <p> The real stakes extend beyond Gaza . What has been @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in UN General Assembly votes , in European courts ruling on arms export licenses , on American campuses , and in Global South capitals is a question of far wider reach : Is international law universal , or is it selective ? Is sovereign equality of states an operational principle or a situational slogan ? Can the legitimacy of an international order durably rest on exemptions granted to certain states by the power that underwrites its architecture ? <p> These questions transcend Palestine . They structure the relationship between North and South , between power and law , between legitimacy and force . South African apartheid lasted forty-six years . It yielded not under the weight of a war , but under growing diplomatic isolation , economic sanctions , internal mobilizations , and a shift in international legitimacy . The mechanism is not mysterious . It is historically documented . What it requires , in the Israeli-Palestinian case , is the same accumulation of constraints -- and the same collective will to apply them without exception of state or power . <p> That moment will come . @@138519602 <h> Memories of the Emergency : From Underground Resistance to Imprisonment <p> I have already written about the Emergency in the previous two parts . Today , I am attempting to write this third instalment . <p> In the 1970s , during Gujarat 's Navnirman movement and the subsequent Bihar Total Revolution movement led by Jayaprakash Narayan , I was 21 years old and a full-time worker of the Rashtra Seva Dal . Inspired by both these movements , I was among those in Maharashtra who tried to organise a similar movement . After the formation of the the Maharashtra Jan Sangharsh Samiti in 1974 at the Wardha Mahila Ashram in the presence of Jayaprakash Narayan , I was made a member of that committee as a Rashtra Seva Dal worker and was trying to build a people 's movement in Maharashtra . <p> During that period , Jayaprakash Narayan personally told me at the Wardha meeting : " Suresh , you should spare some time and come to Bihar as soon as possible to start the work of Rashtra Seva Dal there . The RSS is involved in the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ should be expanded to other parts of the country just like in Maharashtra . Therefore , you must come to Bihar first . " <p> On the night of 25 June 1975 , when the Emergency was declared , I was travelling from Amravati in Maharashtra towards Patna via Nagpur by train , on JP 's invitation . On the morning of 26 June , as soon as the train reached Jabalpur station , I heard passengers whispering that Indira Gandhi had declared the Emergency and arrested Jayaprakash Narayan and all opposition leaders . I immediately picked up my luggage , got down from the train , took a cycle rickshaw to Jabalpur bus stand , and returned to Maharashtra to plunge into underground work against the Emergency . <p> Because of censorship , newspapers were heavily edited . We started bringing out cyclostyled bulletins and distributing them . Around the same time ( 1976 ) , Jayaprakash Narayan announced the formation of the People 's Union for Civil Liberties ( PUCL ) , of which he was the President and Barrister V.M. Tarkunde was the Working President . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to establish the Maharashtra unit of PUCL . S.M. Joshi was made President and I was made Secretary . Our work included secretly distributing cyclostyled pamphlets and literature to awaken the people after the kidnapping of democracy , visiting the families of non-RSS arrested prisoners in jails , studying their family problems , and providing financial help . The RSS had already created its own network to support its own people , while the families of non-RSS and non-Jana Sangh people were in dire straits . That is why the Maharashtra PUCL took this initiative . <p> I prepared a report after visiting families of non-Jana Sangh and non-RSS people in the Vidarbha districts -- Nagpur , Amravati , Wardha , Yavatmal , and Akola -- identifying who needed financial assistance . Some needy families were given help accordingly . <p> In May 1976 , in the scorching heat , we organised a special two-day meeting in the Gramdan village of Keliveli in Akola district , where about 25 -- 30 people gathered to discuss what more could be done against the Emergency . Professor B.L . Bhole from Nagpur @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . After the meeting , we spent a week moving through remote villages in the Satpura hills in Telhara taluka of Akola district , spreading the message . The villagers gave us excellent cooperation and arranged our stay and food . From this , I realised that the terror of the the 1975 Emergency had not reached the villages . People helped us fearlessly . <p> After My Arrest During the Emergency <p> In the first week of October 1976 ( perhaps 5 -- 6 October ) , around 4 -- 5 pm , I reached the office of the Amravati District Sarvodaya Mandal on the motorcycle of my friend Dr. Arun Malpe from Morshi . After getting down , he said he was going to meet his in-laws and asked me to finish my work and be ready so we could return to Morshi before dark . <p> I had just reached the office to check if any correspondence had arrived when there was continuous knocking on the door . First , I went to the balcony and saw a police van parked on the Amravati-Badnera Road . The @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ had surrounded it from all sides . I understood that my one-and-a-quarter years of underground work were coming to an end . <p> When I opened the door , a police officer with other policemen was standing there . After arresting me , he asked for the keys to the almirahs . I said they were with the President of the Sarvodaya Mandal , who had gone to the village . The police broke open all the almirahs , scattered files and materials all over the room , and conducted a search . Then they took me to Rajapeth Police Station . The lock-up was already packed with 20 -- 25 other prisoners . I was pushed in . There was a terrible stench . In a 10 ? 10 room , people were crammed together like passengers in a Mumbai local train during rush hour . <p> At night , half-cooked rotis and pumpkin curry were given . But how to sleep was the problem for everyone . After talking , I learned that , except for me , all the others were pickpockets or petty criminals . I @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the Emergency . <p> Around midnight , I was taken out of the lock-up to another room . I thought I was being shifted to a separate room because of my political activities . But inside , a 100-watt bulb was burning in a 10 ? 10 room with the doors and windows closed . A CID Inspector was sitting on a chair behind a table . He asked me to sit on the chair in front of him and politely asked , " You went from Amravati to the Baroda Dynamite meeting in Mumbai on such-and-such date by such-and-such train . Tell me who else was present at that meeting . " <p> I firmly said , " I never went to Mumbai . So how can I tell you who was there ? " ( Though inside I was shaken because the Inspector was right about my trip to Mumbai . ) <p> The meeting had been held in the flat of Professor Pushpa Bhave and Anant Bhave near Ruia College , within walking distance of Dadar station . @@138534192 <h> The commission on inquiry found that more than 20,000 Palestinian children have been killed and more than 44,000 injured since October 2023 . <p> Palestinians children at the site of Israeli strikes on a house , in Gaza City , on September 26 , 2025 . Ebrahim Hajjaj/ Reuters <p> A recent United Nations report has detailed serious allegations of Israel deliberately targeting Palestinian children during the conflict since October 2023 . <p> The report by the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory , including East Jerusalem and Israel , which has been rejected outright by the Israeli government , documents harrowing child deaths . It describes the scale of the deaths as " unprecedented " . <p> Legally , the report itself does not prosecute anyone , but it could have major consequences by adding to a growing record of international law evidence . <h> An independent investigation <p> The commission is a standing investigative body created by the UN Human Rights Council in May 2021 after the escalation in Gaza and East Jerusalem that year . <p> Its mandate is unusually broad @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ violations of international humanitarian and human rights law in Israel and the Occupied Palestinian Territory , identifying root causes and preserving evidence for accountability . <p> This latest report is significant because it focuses specifically on children , examining the impact of Israeli military operations on Palestinian children between October 2023 and March 2026 . <p> The report notes that the commission sent requests for information to the State of Palestine , the Ministry of Health in the Gaza Strip and the Israeli government . The first two responded , but the latter did not . <h> Four major findings <p> The commission 's report makes four highly significant findings . <p> 1 . The scale of child deaths is unprecedented <p> The report finds more than 20,000 Palestinian children have been killed and more than 44,000 injured since October 2023 . <p> The commission says the " overwhelming scale and rate of children killed and injured in Gaza have been unparalleled across modern conflicts globally " . <p> UNICEF describe the Gaza Strip as " the most dangerous place in the world to be a child " . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ report 's most legally explosive finding . It documents repeated incidents of children being killed by single sniper or drone shots , often in the head or upper torso , suggesting deliberate targeting rather than incidental harm . <p> Cases such as Hind Rajab and other children shot while evacuating or sheltering are central examples . <p> Doctors on medical missions in Gaza reported to the commission that it appeared Israeli Defense Force soldiers were engaged in a " game " of target practice with " different body parts being targeted on different days " . <p> The commission concluded that based on forensic evidence and military analysis , there are reasonable grounds to believe some children were deliberately targeted . <p> 3 . Systematic attacks on child-essential infrastructure <p> The report documents attacks on hospitals , schools and orphanages , which enjoy special protection under international law . The commission found these attacks have directly contributed to preventable child deaths , long-term disability and educational collapse . <p> Schools have been destroyed in the conflict , including this one in May 2025 . Jehad Alshrafi/AP <p> 4 . Arbitrary @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ patterns of child detention , ill-treatment and abuse in custody . <p> The commission noted that dehumanising rhetoric by political leaders , soldiers and public figures has normalised violence against Palestinian children and contributed to an environment where such harm becomes acceptable . <h> How do these findings fit with international law ? <p> This report is important because it reframes the war not only through the lens of civilian casualties , but through special legal obligations owed to children . <p> International humanitarian law and international human rights law apply concurrently in the Occupied Palestinian Territory . This is because Israel retains effective control over its borders , airspace and territorial waters , and has re-established military control on the ground . <p> As an occupying power , Israel has specific obligations under the Fourth Geneva Convention . These include ensuring food , medical care and the protection of civilians , especially children . <p> Under the Convention on the Rights of the Child , Israel must protect children 's rights to life , survival and development . It must prohibit arbitrary detention , torture and deprivation of life @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ child remain a primary consideration in all actions affecting them . <p> The commission 's conclusions are stark : children have not simply been caught in the crossfire of war . Many appear to have been deliberately targeted , denied essential care , detained , tortured , displaced and subjected to conditions that threaten their survival . It reframes the suffering of Palestinian children not as collateral damage alone , but as a possible site of serious international crimes . <h> Serious legal questions <p> If children were deliberately targeted , this would constitute a grave breach of the international humanitarian law principle to distinguish combatants from civilians . <p> The sheer scale of child deaths raises serious concerns about whether Israeli forces have been adhering to the proportionality analysis : if civilian harm is excessive compared with the concrete military advantage anticipated , the attack is unlawful . <p> Parties must take all feasible precautions to minimise civilian harm . The report argues Israel 's use of heavy explosive weapons in densely populated civilian areas indicates repeated failures of precaution . <h> Adding to the evidence record <p> In @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ like this help build the legal architecture for future prosecutions . <p> The findings may feed directly into ongoing investigations by the International Criminal Court into alleged crimes in Palestine . The commission explicitly recommends further scrutiny by the court . <p> States could rely on this evidence in domestic prosecutions under universal jurisdiction . This allows domestic courts to hear cases alleging international crimes , regardless of where the crimes occurred , or the nationality of the victims or perpetrators . <p> States may also impose targeted sanctions or arms embargoes based on credible findings in UN reports documenting serious violations of international humanitarian law , even without a court ruling . <p> The findings could shape arguments in existing and future proceedings before the International Court of Justice , particularly around genocide and occupation . <p> Under international law , children are supposed to be the most protected people in war . The children of Gaza have not just suffered in the war , they have become one of its defining legal fault lines .

@@138546655 <h> When the Children Become the Target <p> On June 23 , the United Nations Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory , including East Jerusalem , and Israel released one of the most devastating reports ever produced by a UN investigative body on the Israeli genocide in Gaza . Its title is almost unbearable to read : The Essence of Childhood Has Been Destroyed . Behind the title lies an accusation of extraordinary gravity . The Commission concludes that Israeli authorities and security forces have deliberately targeted Palestinian children and that these actions amount to genocide , crimes against humanity , and war crimes in the Gaza Strip , alongside war crimes in the occupied West Bank . <p> The report is not an emotional appeal . It is a painstaking legal document built upon witness testimony , forensic evidence , satellite imagery , military analysis , medical records , and years of documentation . What it presents is not merely another catalogue of civilian casualties . It argues that the killing , maiming , starvation , detention and psychological destruction of Palestinian children can not @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ concludes that children themselves have become deliberate targets of Israeli military policy . The implications of such a finding reach far beyond Gaza . They raise fundamental questions about the future of international law itself . <p> A Report of Extraordinary Gravity <p> The Commission estimates that since October 2023 , at least 20,179 Palestinian children have been killed and more than 44,000 injured . Approximately thirty per cent of all Palestinians killed have been children . These figures alone place the Gaza war among the deadliest conflicts for children in modern history . Yet the report 's importance lies not simply in the numbers but in its conclusions regarding intent . <p> It documents repeated instances in which children were shot by snipers , attacked by drones , struck while seeking food or water , or killed despite posing no military threat -- as should have been obvious . It examines the repeated use of high-yield explosives in densely populated civilian areas long after the predictable consequences for children had become undeniable . It details attacks on maternity hospitals , neonatal wards , schools , orphanages and shelters . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ medicine , showing how starvation , disease and the collapse of medical services have become instruments of war directed against an entire civilian population whose youngest members are the most vulnerable . <p> The Commission investigates Israeli detention practices involving Palestinian minors . Children arrested in Gaza and the West Bank describe torture , sexual violence , degrading treatment and disappearance into detention facilities without information being provided to their families . Such abuses , the report concludes , form part of a broader system of collective punishment directed against Palestinian society across generations . The UN Commission report is not novel on this , even though the findings are devastating . They corroborate previous reports by Save the Children ( Palestinian Children in Israeli Military Detention Report Increasingly Violent Conditions , 29 February 2024 ) and , long before this genocidal campaign that began in 2023 by UNICEF ( Children in Israeli Military Detention , February 2013 ) . In his recent book , Survivors of the Darkness , the Palestinian journalist Wesam Afifa documents the horrendous violence of the Israeli concentration camps set up for Palestinians , including @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ conclusion is that the destruction extends beyond physical death . Childhood itself has become a battlefield . Psychological trauma , orphanhood , repeated displacement , hunger , interrupted education and permanent disability together amount to what the Commission describes as the destruction of ' the essence of childhood ' . <p> A Pattern Long Documented <p> The Commission 's findings did not emerge suddenly . For nearly two years , Palestinian journalists have documented children pulled from collapsed buildings , infants dying in incubators without electricity , families wiped out in airstrikes and children shot while attempting to retrieve food or water . Many of those journalists paid with their own lives . Gaza has become the ' deadliest conflict ever for journalists ' , reported Irene Khan , the UN Special Rapporteur on the promotion and protection of the right to freedom of opinion and expression . Yet , despite extraordinary danger the journalists continued documenting events that much of the world preferred not to see . <p> International human rights organisations reached similar conclusions long before this recent UN report . Save the Children repeatedly warned that Gaza @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to be a child . Defence for Children International -- Palestine documented repeated shootings of children in circumstances that raised serious questions about military necessity . Human Rights Watch investigated attacks on schools , hospitals and refugee camps . Amnesty International examined repeated strikes that appeared to violate the principles of distinction and proportionality under international humanitarian law . UNICEF repeatedly warned that children were being killed and injured on an unprecedented scale . None of these organisations described isolated accidents . They identified recurring patterns that demanded independent investigation . The new UN report effectively consolidates this vast body of evidence into a single legal assessment . <p> In January 2024 , the International Court of Justice found that South Africa 's case alleging genocide by Israel was plausible and ordered provisional measures requiring Israel to prevent acts prohibited under the Genocide Convention , preserve evidence , and facilitate humanitarian assistance . Subsequent orders strengthened these requirements as conditions in Gaza deteriorated . Although the Court has not yet ruled on the merits of the genocide case , it has repeatedly recognised the grave risk faced by the Palestinian @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ law . The new Commission report provides further evidentiary material that will inevitably shape future legal proceedings . <p> The Silence of the Israeli State <p> Perhaps equally striking has been the nature of Israel 's response . Rather than seriously engaging with the evidence assembled by the Commission , Israeli officials once again dismissed the report outright , describing it as politically motivated and fundamentally biased . They rejected its conclusions in their entirety without offering substantive rebuttal of the specific incidents , witness testimony , or forensic evidence presented by investigators . Every state has the right to defend itself against allegations . But serious allegations require serious answers . <p> If children were not deliberately targeted , the burden rests upon the Israeli authorities to explain why thousands of children have died in circumstances repeatedly documented by journalists , humanitarian organisations , medical personnel , and now a UN Commission of Inquiry . Why have hospitals , maternity wards , schools and refugee shelters been struck again and again ? Why have humanitarian convoys repeatedly come under attack ? Why have children continued to die even after @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ accountability ? Simply repeating accusations of institutional bias can not substitute for factual explanation . The refusal to engage with evidence has itself become a disturbing feature of this war . <p> International humanitarian law rests upon the principle that states are accountable for their conduct . Accountability becomes impossible when every investigation is dismissed before its evidence is even examined . <p> Justice S. Muralidhar and the Duty of the Judge <p> The findings of the UN Commission also remind us of the importance of judges who understand that the law is not merely a technical instrument but a defence against arbitrary power . Few Indian judges have embodied that principle more consistently than Justice S. Muralidhar , who as UN Commission on Human Rights , chaired this new report 's committee . <p> Justice Muralidhar earned a reputation over decades as one of India 's most respected constitutional jurists , particularly in cases involving civil liberties , communal violence , and the protection of vulnerable communities . He was one of the principal judicial voices in implementing accountability after the 1984 anti-Sikh pogrom , insisting that impunity could @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ inconvenient . His commitment to constitutional duty became internationally known during the communal violence in northeast Delhi in February 2020 . As hospitals struggled to treat victims trapped by the violence , Justice Muralidhar and Justice Anup J. Bhambhani convened an extraordinary midnight hearing at Justice Muralidhar 's residence . The Delhi High Court ordered the police to ensure the safe passage of the injured to hospitals and directed immediate emergency medical treatment . Later that day , Justice Muralidhar sharply questioned the failure of the Delhi Police to register cases against political leaders whose inflammatory speeches had been widely circulated , reminding the authorities that the country could not permit ' another 1984 ' . <p> Within hours of these hearings , the Government of India notified Justice Muralidhar 's transfer to the Punjab and Haryana High Court , although the recommendation for his transfer had formally been made by the Supreme Court Collegium earlier that month . The timing generated widespread concern among lawyers , retired judges , and civil society organisations , who regarded the episode as raising troubling questions about judicial independence . <p> Justice Muralidhar @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ law . Courts do not exist to ratify the conduct of governments . Their function is to examine evidence without fear or favour , especially when the victims are those with the least political power . The same principle animates the work of the UN Commission of Inquiry . Its conclusions may be contested , but they can not simply be dismissed because they are politically inconvenient . The proper response to serious evidence is serious engagement . That is the first obligation of any state that claims to respect the rule of law . <p> The Test Before Humanity <p> The UN Commission 's report is ultimately not only about Israel or Palestine . <p> It asks whether the international legal order created after the defeat of European fascism still possesses the moral authority to defend children from organised violence . If more than 20,000 children can be killed while the institutions of international diplomacy continue largely as normal , then the promise embodied in the Genocide Convention , the Geneva Conventions , and the Convention on the Rights of the Child stands gravely diminished . The report will @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ lives already lost . But it establishes a historical record that will become increasingly difficult to erase . Long after governments change and military campaigns conclude , this record will remain . History remembers those who committed atrocities . It also remembers those who looked away . <h> Subscribe to Our Newsletter <p> Vijay Prashad is an Indian historian and journalist . @@138546691 <h> New Atheism , Western Hegemony , and the Imperial Calculus <p> The turn of the twenty-first century witnessed the meteoric rise of a discursive phenomenon that captured the imagination of the Western reading public and reshaped the landscape of popular intellectual culture . " New Atheism , " spearheaded principally by the evolutionary biologist Richard Dawkins and the neuroscientist Sam Harris -- alongside Christopher Hitchens and Daniel Dennett , the so-called " Four Horsemen " -- emerged from the geopolitical trauma of the September 11th attacks and the subsequent declaration of the " War on Terror . " This movement positioned itself not merely as a philosophical critique of theism , but as an enlightened vanguard defending Western civilisation against the perceived forces of pre-modern , regressive religious fundamentalism . Their books achieved unprecedented commercial success : Dawkins 's The God Delusion ( 2006 ) and Harris 's The End of Faith ( 2004 ) became international bestsellers , transforming atheism from a relatively marginal intellectual position into a global cultural movement ( Bullivant , p.4-8 ) . <p> However , beneath the rhetorical veneer of objective scientific rationalism @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ operated as a profoundly hollow , ahistorical , and apolitical enterprise . Far from constituting a neutral critique of religious dogma , it weaponised the language of Enlightenment rationality to serve specific political ends , functioning as an ideological handmaiden to Western imperialism , American militarism , and neoliberal hegemony . The movement 's " ostensibly ' apolitical ' stance , " as critics have consistently observed , " is in reality a tacit endorsement " of the very power structures it purported to scrutinise . <p> This paper offers a comprehensive and rigorously argued critique of New Atheism . It demonstrates how the movement systematically emptied religion of its material , economic , and historical contexts , thereby producing a flattened , apolitical caricature of global conflict . It examines the movement 's profound moral failures , specifically focusing on its systemic indifference to Palestinian suffering and its uncritical endorsement of Western state violence . It traces the structural alignment between the New Atheist critique of religion and the geopolitical directives of the global North . And it reveals how a movement predicated on intellectual emancipation became an instrument @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the language of reason . <p> The analysis draws upon a broad range of critical perspectives , including postcolonial theory , political geography , sociology of religion , and international relations , to expose the movement 's foundational contradictions . Ultimately , this document argues that the legacy of New Atheism is not one of genuine intellectual liberation or the universal expansion of human freedom . Rather , it stands as a case study in how the language of secularism and scientific rationalism can be co-opted to serve the interests of state violence , imperial expansion , and civilisational supremacy . <p> The Ontological Hollowness of the New Atheist Paradigm <p> The primary philosophical vulnerability of New Atheism lies in its reductionist ontology of religion . Writers such as Dawkins , in The God Delusion , and Harris , in The End of Faith , approach religion almost exclusively as a set of literal , poorly substantiated scientific propositions about the cosmos . To the New Atheist , religion is merely erroneous physics or faulty biology -- a collection of cognitive errors perpetuated by evolutionary misfires , cultural indoctrination , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " virus of the mind , " arguing that religious belief constitutes a form of irrationality that persists largely through cultural inheritance rather than evidence ( Dawkins , The God Delusion , p.176 ) . Harris extends this critique further , asserting that certain religious doctrines can directly motivate violence , and that liberal societies frequently underestimate the dangers posed by theological absolutism ( Harris , p.12-35 ) . <p> This perspective ignores decades of foundational scholarship in the sociology , anthropology , and phenomenology of religion . As Clifford Geertz demonstrated in The Interpretation of Cultures , religion is not simply a list of abstract beliefs held in a vacuum ; it is a complex web of social practices , kinship networks , institutional structures , material realities , and historical memories that together constitute a " system of symbols which acts to establish powerful , pervasive , and long-lasting moods and motivations " ( Geertz , p.90 ) . Talal Asad further complicates the New Atheist framework by arguing that " the assumption that there is a trans-historical and transcultural concept of religion is one that should be @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ) . By treating religion as an isolated cognitive virus -- " memes , " in Dawkinsian terminology -- New Atheism strips the phenomenon of its material substance . <p> William T. Cavanaugh challenges the foundational assumption that religion possesses a unique propensity towards violence , arguing that modern political discourse frequently isolates " religious violence " whilst overlooking analogous forms of violence committed by secular states in pursuit of nationalism , security , or ideological projects ( Cavanaugh , p.1-15 ) . The New Atheist critique is therefore fundamentally hollow : it attacks a theological straw man , wilfully blind to the ways in which religious institutions are deeply intertwined with economic and political realities . <p> What is most revealing about this reductionism is its ideological convenience . By treating religion as an isolated cognitive disease , the New Atheist framework can dispense with the messy , inconvenient realities of geopolitics . It fails to recognise that religious identity often serves as the primary language through which marginalised communities articulate resistance , express grief , or organise solidarity against oppressive structures . The Palestinian who prays in a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Muslim after the destruction of his state , the Afghan who turns to religious institutions after decades of foreign intervention -- none of these figures is adequately described by Dawkins 's " meme " theory . They are historical actors responding to material conditions , not passive dupes of cognitive software . <p> The Idealist Fallacy and Ahistoricism <p> New Atheism is deeply invested in what may be termed the " idealist fallacy " -- the philosophical error of assuming that ideas move history independently of material conditions . Harris frequently asserts that specific theological texts possess an inherent , immutable causal power . In this view , a scriptural passage written in the seventh century can be directly mapped onto the actions of a twenty-first-century actor , completely bypassing intervening variables such as colonial subjugation , economic collapse , military occupation , or state collapse . Harris explicitly rejects the notion that socio-economic factors play any significant role in the rise of religious extremism , asserting that " the rise of Islamic fundamentalism is only a problem because the fundamentals of Islam are a problem " ( Harris , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ vacuum where structural realities disappear entirely . For example , when analysing contemporary geopolitical violence in the Middle East , New Atheists consistently privilege religious texts over historical events . The structural devastation wrought by the Sykes-Picot agreement , the imposition of Western-backed autocracies , the starvation of civilian populations through economic sanctions , the physical destruction of infrastructure in repeated wars of aggression -- all are dismissed as secondary or entirely irrelevant factors . The complex , messy realities of geopolitics are reduced to a simplistic binary : an enlightened , rational West locked in an existential struggle against a backwards , religiously intoxicated East . <p> The sociological literature on terrorism has thoroughly dismantled this idealist framework . Robert Pape 's landmark study , which analysed every instance of suicide terrorism from 1980 to 2003 , conclusively demonstrated that the primary driver of suicide terrorism is not religious fundamentalism but resistance to foreign military occupation ( Pape , p.23 ) . Suicide bombers are overwhelmingly deployed as strategic , asymmetric weapons designed to compel an occupying force to withdraw from a specific homeland . By ignoring this empirical @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ principles of scientific inquiry they claim to uphold . They abandon data in favour of an ideological dogma that weaponises secularism to dehumanise populations under occupation . <p> Dawkins 's assertion in The God Delusion that without religion there would be " no Israeli-Palestinian wars " ( Dawkins , p.259 ) is perhaps the most glaring example of this historical amnesia . This reductionism ignores the pre-existing nationalist and ethnic tensions , the colonial legacy of the Balfour Declaration , the material reality of land dispossession , and the ongoing military occupation that are the concrete drivers of the conflict . By reducing a deeply complex geopolitical struggle to a " delusion , " Dawkins demonstrates a profound inability to analyse the world he seeks to explain ( Foster et al. , p.182 ) . <p> The Apolitical Deception <p> New Atheism presents secularism as a neutral , objective , and universal space where all individuals can meet free from bias . This claim to neutrality is , however , one of the movement 's most consequential and dishonest rhetorical manoeuvres . As the political theorist Wendy Brown has observed @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ religion . Rather , it is a historically specific configuration of power that emerged from the European wars of religion to regulate , discipline , and define what constitutes " acceptable " public behaviour and " primitive " private devotion ( Brown , p.7 ) . Talal Asad similarly contends that secularism " establishes its own distinctions between public and private life , legitimate and illegitimate belief , and acceptable and unacceptable forms of political expression , " distinctions that are " not merely descriptive but involve the exercise of power through legal institutions , educational systems , and state authority " ( Asad , Formations of the Secular , p.181-222 ) . <p> Within this framework , New Atheism may be understood less as the absence of ideology than as the expression of a particular liberal worldview . Its celebration of scientific rationality , individual autonomy , and secular governance reflects values that emerged within specific historical contexts -- principally the experience of post-Enlightenment Western Europe and North America . The movement 's tendency to present these values as culturally unmarked and universally self-evident is not merely intellectually dishonest @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ secular society as the pinnacle of human evolutionary progress , New Atheists successfully insulated the Western state from moral and political critique . The state is cast as an arbiter of neutral rationality , whilst its structural violence -- whether through mass incarceration , racial capitalism , or border militarisation -- is absolved of systemic malice . Under this framework , violence committed by a secular state is always framed as rational , accidental , or a regrettable necessity . Conversely , violence committed by non-Western , non-secular actors is classified as irrational , intrinsic , and driven by a theological lust for death . The asymmetry is not incidental to the New Atheist project ; it is foundational to it . <p> New Atheism emerged in the context of the post-9/11 political climate and the public elevation of security politics . The movement is undeniably political , but its politics are largely framed as culture-war activism against religion , especially in Anglo-American public life , rather than as a broader critique of power . Its campaigns focus on visibility , secular symbolism , school religion , and public ritual @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . This is why the movement can sound radical whilst remaining safe : it attacks clerical authority but rarely interrogates the geopolitical systems that enable violence on a much larger scale . <p> The Reification of the " Civilisational " Binary <p> The apolitical stance of New Atheism is , paradoxically , its most potent political weapon . By pretending to stand above politics , the movement actively naturalised the " Clash of Civilisations " thesis popularised by Samuel Huntington , formerly advisor to Apartheid-era South Africa , who argued that the post-Cold War world would be characterised not by ideological struggles but by cultural conflicts between distinct , monolithic civilisations ( Huntington , p.22 ) . Dawkins and Harris consistently categorise human societies along civilisational lines , where the " West " represents science , free speech , and gender equality , whilst the " Islamic world " represents obscurantism , censorship , and misogyny . <p> Academic analysis of their work has identified a " belligerent geopolitical imagination " that presents the West as " existentially-threatened " and therefore justified in using " extraordinary violence to protect itself @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Atheism inherits this deeply conservative , racially charged framework , merely replacing Huntington 's " Judeo-Christian " terminology with the language of " secular rationalism . " While the right-wing conservatives favour the ' Judeo-Christian ' canard ... the liberals opt for ' new atheism ' ... Both , however , are in perfect agreement about their perceived white supremacy , which supposedly gives them the right to wreak havoc across the world as they please . <p> This binary requires an immense amount of historical amnesia . It requires ignoring how Western powers have historically supported , funded , and armed ultra-conservative religious factions across the global South -- such as the Mujahideen in Afghanistan during the Cold War -- to undermine secular , socialist , or nationalist movements that threatened Western economic hegemony . It requires forgetting that the CIA 's support for Islamist groups was a deliberate strategy to counter Soviet influence , and that the destruction of the secular Ba'athist state in Iraq created the vacuum into which the Islamic State subsequently stepped . By scrubbing these geopolitical manoeuvres from the narrative , New Atheism transforms @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ into a clean , idealised conflict between reason and superstition . <p> Nathan Lean similarly argues that the post-9/11 public sphere created conditions in which criticism of Islam increasingly became detached from broader historical analysis , with public debate focusing upon theology whilst paying comparatively limited attention to colonial legacies , authoritarian governance , foreign intervention , or economic inequalities ( Lean , p.74-101 ) . In this context , the New Atheist emphasis upon religious doctrine appeared to many scholars as analytically incomplete , privileging ideological explanations over historical and political ones . Scholars have observed that neither Dawkins nor Harris speaks Arabic , possesses any formal training in Islamic history , sociology , or Middle Eastern politics , or has spent any meaningful time engaging with the diverse , living communities of the Muslim world . They treat a global population of nearly two billion human beings -- spanning from Senegal to Indonesia , encompassing vast differences in culture , class , politics , and practice -- as a single , monolithic mass moving in lockstep with a literalist interpretation of seventh-century texts . <p> This essentialism is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ old colonial logic of the mission civilisatrice for the twenty-first century . Edward Said 's foundational analysis in Orientalism demonstrates that Western representations of Islamic societies have long been influenced by traditions that portray the East as irrational , despotic , and resistant to progress -- representations that function less as objective descriptions than as ideological narratives reinforcing Western cultural superiority ( Said , p.1-28 ) . Though Dawkins and Harris reject racial prejudice and insist that their criticisms concern ideas rather than peoples , critics contend that their writings reproduce these older civilisational binaries by treating Islam as uniquely resistant to reform or modernity . <p> Indifference to Palestinian Suffering and the Zionist Alibi <p> Nowhere is the moral and analytical bankruptcy of New Atheism more starkly apparent than in its treatment of the Palestinian struggle for self-determination . For both Dawkins and Harris , the ongoing occupation of Palestine is routinely flattened into a religious dispute over sacred real estate . By characterising the issue as an ancient , intractable feud between two competing theological dogmas , New Atheism systematically erases the material reality of settler-colonialism , military @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ This discursive move performs a vital service for the preservation of Western hegemony . When Harris remarks that the Israeli-Palestinian conflict is , at its root , an issue of Islamic extremism , he effectively delegitimises decades of secular Palestinian resistance -- from the early Marxist-Leninist factions of the Palestine Liberation Organisation ( PLO ) to the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine ( PFLP ) and contemporary grassroots , non-violent civil society campaigns . The structural realities of checkpoint networks , illegal settlements , home demolitions , and the blockade of the Gaza Strip are rendered invisible . They are replaced by a monomaniacal focus on the religious rhetoric of Hamas , which is then taken as the authentic , unchanging essence of all Palestinian aspirations . <p> A closer examination of the sources used by the New Atheists reveals a systematic cherry-picking of evidence to support a narrative that exonerates Israel and pathologises Palestinian resistance . Harris 's The End of Faith cites the case of a failed Palestinian suicide bomber to argue that such acts are driven only by the " love of martyrdom " and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ He deliberately omits the context provided in the source material , which details Israeli military raids , the bomber 's desperate economic circumstances , and his stated motivation to resist occupation . Similarly , Dawkins quotes a Palestinian interviewee to emphasise the allure of " jihad , " but ignores the background details concerning the man 's family 's displacement in 1948 and his subsequent imprisonment . Even Hitchens , in God Is Not Great , recounts the murder of a Palestinian woman by Hamas to illustrate religious brutality , yet fails to mention that the source article he cites explains the rise of fundamentalism as a direct consequence of the Israeli occupation . The pattern is consistent and deliberate : religion is extracted from its political and historical context to serve as a singular , de-contextualised cause of violence . <p> Joseph Massad argues that liberal critiques of political Islam frequently separate contemporary conflicts from their historical contexts . The language of secular modernity and universal values can obscure the extent to which colonial histories , military occupation , and geopolitical interests shape present realities . Massad therefore cautions @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ religious belief without giving equal attention to state violence or prolonged systems of political domination ( Massad , p.183-212 ) . Said 's broader argument concerning the representation of the Middle East in Western intellectual life reinforces this point : portrayals of the region have often privileged cultural and religious explanations over historical and political analysis , depicting conflict as the consequence of civilisational difference rather than of concrete political circumstances ( Said , p.300-328 ) . <p> The Ethical Double Standard of State Terror <p> The New Atheist critique exhibits an extraordinary ethical asymmetry when evaluating violence . Harris has argued that the moral status of an action is determined entirely by intention . He contends that because Western democracies and Israel do not explicitly intend to kill civilians -- seeking only to target combatants -- their killing of thousands of non-combatants via aerial bombardment is morally superior to the actions of non-state actors who intentionally target civilians . This focus on subjective intention functions as an ethical alibi for state-sanctioned mass violence . It ignores the structural predictability of high-altitude bombing campaigns in densely populated urban centres , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ certainties . <p> In a widely discussed public lecture , Harris argued that the conflict is fundamentally asymmetrical not in terms of military power -- where Israel possesses one of the most advanced , Western-subsidised war machines on earth -- but in terms of moral standing . Harris asserts that " ordinary human beings " exist only on the Israeli side of the ledger , whilst the Palestinian population is thoroughly compromised by a collective religious pathology . This represents a moral obscenity dressed in the language of reason : a neuroscientist using the authority of science to deny the full humanity of a people living under military occupation . <p> Harris has further argued that Western democracies possess a rational , secularised public sphere whose intentions in global warfare are fundamentally benevolent , even when their actions result in catastrophic civilian casualties . When a Western liberal democracy drops thousands of bombs on civilian populations , launches illegal invasions , destabilises sovereign nations , and runs extrajudicial torture sites like Abu Ghraib or Guantanamo Bay , these actions are categorised as tragic tactical missteps or necessary measures for defending civilisation . <p> Harris has also deployed his media platform to sneer at and dismiss warnings of ethnic cleansing and genocide in Gaza , characterising these grave legal and moral inquiries as a " new blood libel " against the Israeli state . By reducing the structural destruction of Palestinian life , infrastructure , universities , and hospitals to a mere " clash of cultures " where " real civilisation " exists only on one side , Harris functions as a high-status Western broadcaster providing intellectual cover for mass atrocities . Palestinian suffering is minimised as an unfortunate secondary consequence of civilisation defending itself , whilst the state violence that inflicts that suffering is laundered as rational and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ right to self-defence and remained focused on religious elements on both sides rather than the political economy of occupation . This " on the fence " posture is precisely the problem : pity is not the same as opposition to the system producing the suffering . The New Atheist movement 's selective outrage -- vigorous condemnation of Islamic practices elsewhere , muted ambivalence about the structural violence of the Israeli state -- reveals a hollowness at the ethical core of its universalist pretensions . <p> Uncritical Endorsement of Western Militarism <p> Far from acting as independent , free-thinking sceptics , the prominent figures of New Atheism frequently operated as rhetorical foot soldiers for the consolidation of American empire . In The End of Faith , Harris formulated arguments that directly legitimised the most extreme manifestations of the War on Terror . He proposed thought experiments justifying the use of torture in ticking-bomb scenarios , arguing that if we are willing to accept the collateral damage of conventional warfare , we should logically accept the precise application of physical torture . The philosophical architecture of this argument is revealing : it @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ arbiters of existential violence and works outward to justify ever more extreme measures . <p> This " security imagination " pervades New Atheist discourse . Harris defends torture by arguing from the permissibility of collateral damage in war towards the permissibility of severe coercion in exceptional cases , thereby folding ethical judgement into a strategic calculus of security . That move is politically significant because it naturalises the state 's violent prerogatives whilst reserving outrage for religious extremism . By prioritising the self-professed " good intentions " of the hegemon over the actual , material results of its actions -- to the Palestinian mother whose child is killed by a Western-supplied missile , the " intent " of the pilot is a meaningless abstraction -- Harris provides a moral alibi for imperial expansion . <p> Moreover , Harris has argued for racial profiling at airports , suggesting that anyone who " looks like he or she could conceivably be Muslim " should be subjected to additional scrutiny . Explanations centred upon extremist belief often marginalise the roles played by foreign occupation , authoritarian alliances , economic inequality , and regional instability . Consequently , military intervention appears as a rational response to irrational violence instead of one factor within a more complex historical process ( Kundnani , p.150-179 ) . New Atheism thus serves a structural function within the ideological apparatus of the empire : it provides the secular , progressive-seeming rationale for positions that would otherwise appear nakedly imperialist . <p> Christopher Hitchens and the Neoconservative Alliance <p> Whilst Dawkins and Harris often claimed to be politically liberal or centrist , their ideological output converged seamlessly with the agenda of neoconservative war architects .
